The Preface to the work titled *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by the Great High Preceptor Śrī Hemādri.

This is the *Pariśiṣṭa* (Supplement) treatise, which is divided into five sections: the *Vrata-khaṇḍa*, the *Dāna-khaṇḍa*, the *Kāla-khaṇḍa*, the *Śrāddha-khaṇḍa*, and the *Pratiṣṭhā-khaṇḍa*. Of these, the *Cintāmaṇi* constitutes the *Dāna-khaṇḍa*; thus it is said:
This volume has been printed and edited by me, Ālūṇa, a former teacher of Smṛti-śāstra at the Saṃskṛta Vidyā Mandira, with the permission of the honorable President of the Ṭikāsī Society;
it is the great treatise on Smṛti, the Caturvargacintāmaṇi, concerning Brāhmaṇas and others.

The sixfold duties of the castes, the students of the Veda, the stages of life, and the mixed castes born of both natural and inverse unions have been determined by way of instruction; however, because they are exceedingly extensive and generally achievable only through great wealth and effort, they are here summarized.

Because it was impossible for him to write it himself, and because its circulation was sparse, ordinary people relied upon common reports and practices to understand it without doubt.
Since it was impossible to distribute [the work] otherwise, out of compassion and for the benefit of all people,

this has been printed using funds provided for that purpose rather than for personal profit; indeed, by the printing of this work, a great service to the Hindu community is expected to be rendered through its widespread application.
Thus it is said; now it is made known that Hemādri, like Devagiri, was the royal court of justice for the emperor Mahādeva, the sovereign lord of the Yādavas;
and Mādrin, himself a king, whose court scholar was Mahāmahī—

The teacher was Śrī Vopadeva; it is inferred that he was born in the Śaka year measured by the five [senses], the moon [one], and the earth [one] (1115), with a variation of three years due to intercalary months. Hemādri also obtained that very same [year]; and this is the well-known tradition: the author of this work is Śrī Vopadeva.

Thus, having raised the verse from the work titled *Padārthādarśa* composed by Vopadeva at numerous places, and having explained that verse according to its true meaning as a constituent part [of the system], it is understood through such compositions as the *Nirṇayasindhu*— beginning with the passage "The root [text] is to be examined in the Hemādri"— that its authority is established.
O Māyā, although it was more appropriate to first seal the section on observances (*vrata-khaṇḍa*) as it followed in sequence,

I have instead sealed the section on gifts (*dāna-khaṇḍa*) out of order; for what is the reason for this, in order to dispel the doubt of the seeker who wonders why only one [section] of the *vrata-khaṇḍa* has become unavailable?
The book has been obtained; four manuscripts of the *Dānakhaṇḍa* have been acquired.

For this reason, although it was the turn for yours to be printed, it was deemed inappropriate to proceed with the printing based on the inspection of only a single manuscript. However, of the four manuscripts—Sanskrit...
One [manuscript] was kept in the library of the Vidyāmandira at Śobhāvāḍājara, the residence of the illustrious Rājendra-nārāyaṇa Vāhādūra; another was in the library of the Asiatic Society;
and with reference to these, the manuscript from Uttarājavāṭau was obtained.
The Chinese version appears; there is a contradiction between the four manuscripts in certain respects, some verses are missing in some places, and in other places they are deficient;
in certain parts the letters are lost—yet even in such a state, [the text remains] extensive.

Although this work has been printed after exerting great effort to examine the mutual readings of the *Manu* and other *Saṃhitās*, as well as the *Smṛti-nibandhas* such as those of Smārta, and after thoroughly investigating and stabilizing the meanings found among neighboring scholars; nevertheless...

This, Ānanda, is the seventh great miracle of the Tathāgata. [The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, having caused his disciples to attain arhatship, enters parinirvāṇa, at that moment, Ānanda, the great earth trembles, shakes, and quakes in six ways; it moves, rises, and falls; it moves toward the east and sinks in the west, and so on up to the four directions. This, Ānanda, is the eighth great miracle of the Tathāgata. [The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, having entered parinirvāṇa, and his relics have been distributed, at that moment, Ānanda, the great earth trembles, shakes, and quakes in six ways; it moves, rises, and falls; it moves toward the east and sinks in the west, and so on up to the four directions. This, Ānanda, is the ninth great miracle of the Tathāgata. [The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when the Tathāgata’s relics are enshrined in a stūpa and worshipped by gods and humans, at that moment, Ānanda, the great earth trembles, shakes, and quakes in six ways; it moves, rises, and falls; it moves toward the east and sinks in the west, and so on up to the four directions. This, Ānanda, is the tenth great miracle of the Tathāgata.”

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who dwells in suffering and seeks suffering; the person who dwells in suffering and seeks happiness; the person who dwells in happiness and seeks suffering; and the person who dwells in happiness and seeks happiness. And how, monks, does one dwell in suffering and seek suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a low family—a family of outcastes, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or flower-removers—a family that is poor, destitute, and lacking in livelihood, where food and clothing are obtained with great difficulty. He is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored; he is weak, sickly, and afflicted by many ailments; he is short-lived, often struck by calamities, and possessed of little wisdom. This is called dwelling in suffering. Furthermore, he engages in unwholesome bodily conduct, unwholesome verbal conduct, and unwholesome mental conduct. Having engaged in such unwholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower realms, or in hell. This is called seeking suffering. Thus, monks, one dwells in suffering and seeks suffering. And how, monks, does one dwell in suffering and seek happiness? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a low family... [as above] ...and possessed of little wisdom. This is called dwelling in suffering. Furthermore, he engages in wholesome bodily conduct, wholesome verbal conduct, and wholesome mental conduct.

Having engaged in such wholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. This is called seeking happiness. Thus, monks, one dwells in suffering and seeks happiness. And how, monks, does one dwell in happiness and seek suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a high family—a family of kshatriyas, brahmins, or householders—a family that is wealthy, affluent, and possessing abundant wealth and grain, where food and clothing are easily obtained. He is handsome, attractive, and well-favored; he is strong, healthy, and free from many ailments; he is long-lived, rarely struck by calamities, and possessed of great wisdom. This is called dwelling in happiness. Furthermore, he engages in unwholesome bodily conduct, unwholesome verbal conduct, and unwholesome mental conduct. Having engaged in such unwholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower realms, or in hell. This is called seeking suffering. Thus, monks, one dwells in happiness and seeks suffering. And how, monks, does one dwell in happiness and seek happiness? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a high family... [as above] ...and possessed of great wisdom. This is called dwelling in happiness. Furthermore, he engages in wholesome bodily conduct, wholesome verbal conduct, and wholesome mental conduct. Having engaged in such wholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. This is called seeking happiness. Thus, monks, one dwells in happiness and seeks happiness. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : :

O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding the four castes and the four stages of life,
I shall proclaim the duty of giving (dānadharma) exactly as it was spoken by the Lord.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "They highly praise giving; giving alone is the supreme refuge. Giving is the kinsman of human beings, for giving is the unsurpassed treasury."
Generosity is the supreme wealth, and generosity is like a mother and father;
without generosity, no desired fruit whatsoever can be attained.
Even for a mere tip of a hair, no scale can be found to weigh it; therefore, one should take refuge in giving, for there is no limit to the merit of those who possess the habit of generosity.
The supreme palace was filled with the resonant sound of necklaces and anklets;
indeed, the perfection of the quality of beauty is obtained through generosity alone.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "Nothing is seen in the three worlds that is superior to giving;
by giving one attains heaven, and by giving alone is prosperity obtained."
By giving one conquers enemies; by giving, disease is destroyed.
Through giving, knowledge is obtained; through giving, one gains the company of young women.
Giving is remembered as the supreme means for achieving virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Uśanas said: For a wealthy person, there is no other service superior to giving;

The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 1:

Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī, having bestowed his own two eyes upon a brahmin,
attained incomparable fame both in this world and the next.

With his frame polished and his cage radiant,

And the royal sage Mahasraji, of great renown,
having renounced his dear life for the sake of a brahmin, went to the unsurpassed worlds.

the high-minded Śatadyumna went to heaven after granting it to Mudgala.

For some indeed attain heaven through acts of charity, sacrifices, and the procreation of offspring.
Through giving, beings are brought under one's control; through giving, even enmities go to their destruction;

The Second Chapter. Now, the nature of giving is described by one who follows the path of the ancient masters of good conduct, through [the presentation of] pure and distinguished [gifts].
The universe attains stability through the multitude of acts performed by those who engage in *ṛta* (sacrificial rites) and *pūrta* (charitable works).
Now, this very Hemādri Sūri— freed from all defects and possessing a mind as pure as the friendship of various wise men— declares this section concerning the nature of various types of gifts.
Devala says: The faithful bestowal of wealth upon a worthy recipient when the opportunity arises is designated as "giving" (dāna); its explanation is now being told.

‘Udite’ means as prescribed by the scriptures. ‘The presentation of objects’ (arthānāṃ pratipādanaṃ) refers to a renunciation that extends to the establishment of the relationship between owner and recipient (svasvāmibhāva) for each respective vessel. “Giving is said to have two causes, six bases, six limbs, and to be associated with maturation; it is of four kinds, three types, and has three forms of destruction. The commentary on this has been stated by that very same author: "In that regard, neither the smallness nor the greatness of a gift brings about prosperity; rather, it is faith and devotion that cause the increase or decrease of gifts."
"Faith" (yā) is the conviction in the existence [of God]. "Devotion" (bhakti) is contemplation preceded by affection.

In the reading "power" (śakti), it means magnanimity. Regarding "having six bases" (ṣaḍadhiṣṭhāna): it is that which has "six bases," meaning diseases, as its instrumental cause; thus it is so described.
Dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as modesty, joy, and fear—
these six are declared to be the foundations of gifts.

He distinguishes them as follows: that which is given daily from one's vessels, regardless of any specific purpose, solely with the intention of renunciation—that is called *yajña-dāna*.

"Without regard for a motive" means without seeking a visible result. They say that what is given incidentally, having indeed regarded a motive, is "gift for the sake of an object," which has its cause in worldly results.
That which is given out of attachment to women, drinking, hunting, and gambling,
or to those who are unworthy, is called "the gift of desire."
When, out of shame in an assembly, one requests from those seeking to honor their teacher and then bestows that gift,
it is known as the "gift of shame" (vrīḍādāna).
That which is given joyfully upon seeing or hearing pleasant things,
those who contemplate Dharma call that gift "the gift of joy" (harṣadāna).
That which is given to those who cause suffering as a means of countering abuse,
misfortune, and violence is called the gift of fearlessness.
Regarding the "sixfold [dharma]": the giver, the recipient, faith, the object to be given, the merit (dharma), and the place and time—these they know as the six limbs of gifts.
He explains them as follows: "Free from disease, virtuous in nature, intent on giving, pure, and possessing an irreproachable livelihood—the giver who possesses these six qualities is praised."

Free from disease, devoid of ailments such as consumption (rājayakṣmā) and the like; possessing the three powers, having a simple livelihood, being modest, and having all his senses intact; liberated from defects of birth—such a Brāhmaṇa is called a worthy recipient (pātra).

Regarding "triśukta": he whose three [qualities]—namely, possession of knowledge, lineage, and purity—are "śuktāni," meaning pure, is thus described. "Ghṛṇālaḥ" means compassionate. "Sakalendriyaḥ" means having unimpaired sense faculties.
Hemādri: Chapter 2 of the Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), pages 46–46.
When there is constant and extreme joy at the sight of supplicants, beginning with a cheerful countenance, as well as hospitality and freedom from envy— that is proclaimed as faith (śraddhā).
Wealth acquired through effort— whether it be small or vast— that causes no harm to others and involves no affliction, is said to be "givable."
If that which is auspicious is difficult to obtain here, or if it occurs at a time when one is worthy of giving, then those place and time are excellent; otherwise, they are not.
Due to the excellence of the state, place, time, recipient, giver,
and offering, even that which is inferior may become superior, or that which is superior may become otherwise.
He states the nature of the sixfold maturation: "Bad fruit, fruitless, inferior, equal, extensive, and inexhaustible—these six are taught as the pairs of maturation according to their ripening."

He explains these [verses]: "That which is given to an atheist, a thief, a violent person, an adulterer, one who has fallen from his caste, a slanderer, or a killer of an embryo, shall bear evil fruit."
"Bad fruit" means a disagreeable result. A gift that is devoid of faith yields a great and bitter fruit.
A gift that causes harm to others will lead even the recipient to a state of deficiency.

‘Niṣphalaṃ’ means having inferior fruit. However, if it were absolutely fruitless, the statement regarding fruit would be untenable for the sake of the other meaning— that whatever one performs with vigor becomes more powerful.

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the term "maturation" (*vipāka*). The word "supreme" (*param*) means "most excellent. And the phrase "the state of being born" (*janatvam ca*) intends something new; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of redundancy with what preceded it.
As it has been said: "Even that which was given, if with a defiled mind..."
However, due to the fault of improper intention, that [act] will yield a fruit equal to that of a gift.
When endowed with all six constituent factors, giving shall result in vast prosperity.

A gift given out of compassion shall lead to inexhaustibility.

"Compassion (anukrośa) means pity (dayā). He states that it is of four kinds: constant (dhruva), habitual (ājasrika), optional (kāmya), and occasional (naimittika), respectively. This Vedic path of giving is described by the twice-born as being fourfold."
Water-stalls, groves, tanks, and so forth, which yield the fruit of all desires,
are certainly called the "triple daily" when they are given day after day.
If that which is desired for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, women, or children is given as a gift established upon desire,
it is designated as "kāmya" (optional or desire-based).

It is traditionally taught that the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is threefold— dependent on time, dependent on action, and dependent on purpose— and is described as being either accompanied by an oblation (*sahoma*) or devoid of an oblation (*homavarjita*).
He states the threefold nature: "Nine are superior, four are middling according to their prescriptions, and the remaining are inferior; they know this to be the threefold nature."
He explains that very point: sour curd, honey, a cow, land, gold, a horse, and an elephant—these are the supreme gifts, by virtue of being gifts of the most excellent substances.
The gift of knowledge, dwellings, objects of enjoyment, and medicines—
these are the intermediate gifts here, due to the giving of intermediate substances.
Regarding "objects of enjoyment": these are the means for enjoyment, such as beds, seats, and so forth.
Sandals, swings, vehicles, umbrellas, drinking vessels, and seats;
lamps, wood, fruits, and the like—these last [categories] may be many years old.
Because the varieties of objects to be given are numerous, enumeration is not desired among the remaining gifts;
therefore, the wise know all other gifts to be inferior.
"Bahuvārṣika" means that which has reached many years, that is to say, ancient.
By this it is shown that even excellent things such as elephants and horses become inferior when they have reached a state of decay.

He speaks of the nature of destruction: "What is sacrificed, given, or studied perishes through repeated recitation;

Therefore, one should not boast in vain of the merit performed by oneself;

"Lāvā" means praise; "vṛthā" means apart from purposes such as protection and so forth. From the Kūrma Purāṇa: "That which is given day after day to one who has rendered no assistance is said to be *nitya*, *naimittika*, *kāmya*, and *vimala*."
That which is given with reference to a specific goal (dhanu) shall have that as its fruit;
however, that which is given into the hands of the learned for the sake of pacifying sin is constant (nityaka).
That gift which is performed by the virtuous for a specific purpose is designated as *naimittika*.
The phrase "by the pacification of evil" is an indication of a specific cause.
That gift which is bestowed for the sake of offspring, victory,
sovereignty, or heaven is declared by the sages who contemplate dharma to be "kāmya" (desire-based) charity.
That gift which is bestowed upon those who know Brahman for the sake of pleasing the Lord,
with a mind endowed with devotion, is stainless and auspicious.
Manu says: "With whatever disposition one bestows whatever gift, with that very same disposition one receives it in return when honored."
"By whatever state of being"— whether sattvic, rājasic, and so forth—
it has been stated in the Bhagavadgītā: "That gift which is given with the thought, 'It ought to be given,' to one who does not return the favor,
at the proper place and time, and to a worthy recipient— that gift is remembered as sāttvika."
But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, or with a view toward a fruit, or again, which is given with distress, is remembered as being of the nature of passion (rājasa).
*vādinaḥ* is an alternative reading.
Hemādri. [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 2]
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, to unworthy recipients, without being consecrated, and with contempt— that is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
From the Viṣṇudharmottara: Actions performed devoid of prescribed rules, or for the purpose of deceiving another, by one overcome by anger and greed, should be designated as tāmasa.
O twice-born one, those performed here with supreme faith become characterized by goodness (sāttvika);
however, a human being who performs tamasic acts always experiences the fruit of such actions as an animal.

Whether through the refinement of one's caste, or again in old age, or in childhood, or even in the state of servitude— no doubt should be entertained here; otherwise, for those of a rajasic nature, the fruit of their human existence would be contrary to what is heard [in the scriptures].
One enjoys the fruit of meritorious deeds in the state of divinity; of this there is no doubt.
From the Matsya Purāṇa: O best of men, for some individuals whose previously performed karma is of a *sāttvika* nature, the fruit is seen even without human effort (*pauruṣa*).

know that the fruit of the tamasic person is likewise obtained through arduous action.
From the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: Giving is considered to be threefold—bodily, vocal, and mental. That which consists of the giving of gold and other such things to an Arhat is considered bodily giving.
"O twice-born ones, the statement 'I grant fearlessness to those who are distressed' is known as verbal [giving];
that which is given by a yogin through this very knowledge is mental giving."

Hārīta states: Giving of improper things is excluded from the category [of valid gifts]; that gift which one regrets after having given is fruitless; and that which one gives to a benefactor is merely a source of affliction; and that which is accompanied by guile (*sopadha*)—[another reading is *yoga*].
Alternatively, there is a reading: "There is no heaven in the giving of intoxicating substances.

The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 2:
Hemādri.
That which is given when solicited yields little fruit; that which is given to an unworthy recipient is an undesirable gift;
that which is proclaimed after being given; that which is given with a smirk; and that which is given without faith are demonic gifts.

That which one gives out of anger is Rākṣasa; that which one gives after reviling, or reviles after having given, is Paiśāca; that which one gives with contempt, or treats with contempt after having given, is Yājña; that which one gives to a dying person is Tāmasa;
and that which one who is not of refined character gives—these are the defects of giving, by which a gift is defiled.
It is unestablished (*asiḍa*), unrelated (*asambaddha*), not leading to heaven (*asvarga*), disgraceful (*ayaśasya*), unstable (*adhruva*), or fruitless (*aphala*).

"Giving at that very time" (*tadānam*) means the offering of the substance being given at the very moment of the resolve (*saṃkalpa*). "To one who has rendered assistance" (*upakāriṇe*) means with the desire for a reciprocal favor. "Only that much" (*tanmātram*) means exactly as much as was given. "Medicinal herb" (*auṣadham*).
That which is accompanied by conditions such as affection (*sneha*) and so forth is called "requested" (*abhyarcita*); it is proclaimed for the sake of worldly understanding.

"Giving what is undesirable" (*aniṣṭadāna*) is giving to an enemy. "Giving out of pride" (*smayadāna*) refers to a specific state of mind such as thinking, "There is no other donor like me"; that which is given with such [a motive] is pride-giving. "Uncommon" (*aprākṛta*) refers to those who are intoxicated and so forth.

In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: One should always understand the great gifts (mahādāna) and the supreme gifts (atidāna), as well as merit consisting of iṣṭa and pūrta, and that which is a fruitless gift (vṛthādāna), with diligence.
The "great gifts" (*mahādāna*) are the sixteen [gifts] to be described hereafter, beginning with the *tanāpuruṣa*. [Namely:
gold, a horse, sesame seeds, an elephant, a female slave, a chariot, land, a house, a maiden, and a tawny cow—these are indeed the ten great gifts.
In the Sāmaveda Upaniṣad: "They say there are three gifts that bestow delight—cows, land, and Sarasvatī; through chanting, sowing, and milking, they indeed deliver one from hell."
Śaṅkha: He who should sacrifice with the *iṣṭis*, the animal sacrifices (*paśubandhas*), and the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsyas*)—
[regarding whom] there is either the reading "announced by another" (*anya-śrāvita*) or,
in some places, the reading "well-known" (*prasiddha*).
In that case, even though the placing of the hand is possible immediately after the relinquishing, there is the reading "taking" (*ādānam*) or "non-offering" (*asamarpaṇam*).
There is also an alternative reading: "one who assists in times of distress" (*vyasanopakāriṇi*).

that which is useful for trade is for a Vaiśya; and that which is useful for craft is for a Śūdra."
Whatever substance is useful to someone should be given to that very person;
and by whichever vessel a person's livelihood is said to be sustained, [that should be provided].
A wise person desiring merit should give each of these to him alone:
a staff, a black antelope skin, and likewise, O brahmins, a water-pot.
By giving these to those who are celibate students, a steadfast person attains great merit:
clothing, bedding, a seat, grain, a house, and household furnishings.
For a householder, however, it should be known that giving these always yields great fruit:
wild rice, bark garments, vegetables, fruits, roots, and cow's milk products.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3] That which is given to a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is proclaimed to be infinite;
likewise, the gift of alms to an ascetic (yati) and the gift of a worthy vessel (pātra) are considered beneficial.
Fragrant substances, auspicious items, betel, red garments, and so forth—these should be given to women; they must be presented into the hands of their husbands, and not otherwise.
Indeed, this is declared to be a secret means of gathering [support]:
providing food and shelter to travelers yields great fruit.
O knower of dharma, he who provides the means for the successful completion of rites such as marriage at the time of their performance shall obtain the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
By giving wealth to the afflicted, a gift becomes of great fruit;
likewise, by giving children’s toys and delicious food.
A man who gives delicious food to those desiring delicious food obtains a captivating fruit, even the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O best of the twice-born, by giving food to one who is bereft of fortune, one obtains inexhaustible fruit and goes to the heavenly world.
O Brahmins, a man who knows the Dharma and possesses great merit attains auspicious and splendid garments; yet even such men, when fallen from their prosperity, become objects of supreme compassion.
Compassion must be shown toward him by those who abide on the path of the virtuous,
having applied diligence when a task for others has arisen.
One obtains inexhaustible fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this matter—by the gift of fodder to brahmins who possess cows.
Those who know the Dharma hear that the fruit of salt is inexhaustible;
likewise for what is given during childbirth, or when one is afflicted by calamity, pain, or fear.
That gift is declared to be inexhaustible for a wise man.
The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 2:
Cīmadri.
O tiger among Brahmins, by giving a water vessel to one who seeks food, one obtains an inexhaustible fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Aṅgiras: Merit should be diligently bestowed upon the gods, upon teachers, and likewise upon one’s mother and father; it has never been taught that demerit should be given.
In the Mandipurāṇa: "A man who gives evil always receives evil a hundred-thousandfold;
one who gives merit receives merit by the hundreds and thousands."
Likewise, through the excellence of the recipient, the gift becomes increasingly superior;
for that which is given to one's father, mother, guru, or a teacher of the Veda [yields great fruit].
One should know that the merit or indeed the demerit is multiplied by a hundred thousand.
In the *Ṣaṭipurāṇa*: "There are these two persons in the world who pierce the solar orb:
one who gives food during a famine, and one who gives gold and clothing during times of plenty."
Now follows the determination of what is not to be taken.
Devala says: Even if one gives away the entire earth acquired through unjust means, if it is given to an unworthy recipient, one shall not obtain even a particle of merit.
From the Vahni Purāṇa: "The wise man who, desiring merit, performs a sacrifice after having accepted wealth acquired through improper means, does not enjoy the fruit of that dharma."
Furthermore, that evil-souled man who is a hypocrite regarding the Dharma gives gifts to the Brahmins for the purpose of gaining the world's trust.
A Brahmin who, having acquired wealth through sinful action,
is deprived of his inheritance and whose mind is possessed by passion and delusion, shall attain a defiled womb.
One who has fallen under the sway of greed and delusion due to the accumulation of wealth,
being evil-minded, torments living beings through violence.
Thus, he who, out of greed, sacrifices and gives away wealth that has been acquired [in this manner]—
Hemādri. [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3]
On account of that evil deed, he does not attain success because of the ancient tradition.
Likewise: "Those rites which are undertaken with these and many other riches acquired through unjust means—in those cases, the Piśācas are the presiding deities."

Vṛṣa-Śātātapa says: He who performs funeral rites for the sake of the deceased with wealth acquired by unjust means does not obtain the fruit thereof, because that wealth was obtained through an illicit source.

In the Skanda Purāṇa: "The property of the gods, the property of the guru, and the property of Caṇḍeśvara—these three types of downfall are seen to result from giving it away, violating its trust, or consuming it."
Yama said: "That donor who gives away the wealth of another after having stolen it goes to hell; the fruit of that gift belongs to the one whose wealth it was."
Likewise: "That which has been used, that which is treated with contempt, that which is insufficient, or that which is unrefined—if one gives such things to Brahmins, it remains as ashes."

"Paribhukta" refers to items such as clothing that have already been used. "Aparyāpta" refers to things incapable of performing their intended function, such as an old ox. Śātātapa states: "Wealth designated for the sale of the Vedas, and that which is acquired from women..."
That which is received from a eunuch is not to be offered to the ancestors or the gods.
(Vedavikrayaḥ means that which is pointed out or designated as the sale of the Vedas. (In the reading *nirviṣṭam*, the meaning is "obtained from the sale of the Vedas.
"'And that which is acquired from women' means by means of subsisting on the occupation of women."

As for what has been acquired: some say it refers to those sold among women. Dakṣa says: "Common property, that which was requested, a deposit, a pledge, wives, their wealth, a thing lent for use, a sealed deposit, and one's entire estate—these cannot be divided as long as there is a male descendant."
Even in times of distress, the wise should not give away these nine things;
the foolish man who gives them away is generally considered to be a sinner.
The Section on Giving, Chapter 3:
Hemādri.

"Common property" (*sāmānyam*) means that which has multiple owners. "Borrowed" (*yācitam*) refers to items such as clothing or ornaments that have been requested and brought for the purpose of social interaction.

"Deposit" (*nyāsa*) refers to property placed in the hands of a householder's kinsmen with the instruction: "Having shown it to the owner of the house, it must be returned to the owner in his absence. "Mortgage" (*ādhi*) is well known. "Wife" (*dārāḥ*) means a spouse. "Wealth" (*tanam*)...
And that has been explained by Manu:
"The wife's property consists of what was received at the fire, what was received as a dowry, and what was given as a token of affection."
What is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman.
*Adhyagya* is that which is given to a woman in the presence of the fire;
*adhyāvāhanika* is that which is given by her father or others at the time of marriage;
*prītikarmaṇi* is that which is presented by the husband on account of his affection for the woman.
Even after marriage, that which is "obtained" from brothers and others [is her property].

Yājñavalkya also says: "That obtained from a brother, a mother, a father, or a husband; that received before the nuptial fire; and that given upon supersession—this is declared to be the woman's wealth."

"That which was given by a husband desiring another wife is 'adhivedanika'; such a kind of woman's property (strīdhana) should not be given. "Anvāhita" is that property which, having been placed in the hand of one person, is subsequently deposited in the hand of another with the instruction, "Give this back to the owner."
"Deposit" (*nikṣepa*) is property placed in the presence of the householder.
Kātyāyana states: "Wives and sons, as well as one's entire property, should not be led away [into sale or gift] against their will; however, one may employ them for oneself."
In times of distress, however, giving away or even selling [the sacred objects] must be performed;
otherwise they cannot be utilized—this is the certain conclusion of the scriptures.
(But in times of distress, giving or even selling [is permitted]; this refers to one's own wife and other such property regarding which one has the desire to give or sell).
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3].
As for the statement regarding wives—that they are not to be given away even in times of distress—this refers to their status as being once given, they are not to be taken back.
This refers to cases such as a wife who is unwilling to give herself or sell herself.
Vasiṣṭha states: "A person is produced from semen and blood, having the mother and father as his cause;
in the giving, selling, or abandoning of him, the mother and father have authority, but not over an only son."

One may give away or receive a son in adoption, for he is for the sake of the lineage of the ancestors; however, a woman may not give away or receive a son except with the permission of her husband. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
If that which was given as a religious gift to some petitioner should later turn out not to be so,
it ought not to have been given to him.

The meaning is that if one gives something to a person who requests it for the purpose of performing a religious duty (*dharma*), but that person does not perform the duty, then it should not have been given to him.
Aṅgiras says: "A cow, a house, a bed, and women should not be given to many [at once]."
When the sacrificial fee has been distributed, the Hotṛ priest indeed causes the donor to cross over [to the other shore].
One [cow] should be given to one person, and never to many;
having fallen into the state of being sold, she burns the donor's family down to the seventh generation.
(This demonstration of fault applies only to the seller, not to the donor under discussion.
Āpaka-yana states: "The daughter, the bed, the house, as well as cattle, women, and so forth—these should be given to a single person;
they must never be given to many."

Vyāsa says: A man should not give to a Brahmin a cow that is deformed, one that does not bear calves, one that is barren, one that is emaciated, one whose offspring has died, one that is dwarfed, or one that miscarries.
A *vehat* is one who destroys the fetus.
Devala states: "By giving a cow that has no calf, one that is diseased, emaciated, leaking [uterine fluids], terrifying with its horns, or whose body and limbs are wasted by thieves, one incurs sin."
Kātyāyana says: One should never, under any circumstances, give land that is saline or barren.
[Chapter 3: Section on Gifts]
Hemādri says:
[One should not reside] in a place surrounded by cremation grounds, nor in one frequented by evildoers.
"Evil ones" refers to predatory creatures such as tigers and the like.
[This is stated] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "One should avoid ground inhabited by thieves, snakes, and likewise by predatory beasts. (53)
But the best of the twice-born should not give that which does not reside in the joints.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "A man who commits a sin always incurs a hundred-thousandfold sin;
therefore, a wise person should never bestow a transgression upon anyone."
In the Mahābhārata: "For toward beings already afflicted by death, disease, old age, and the like, what other person who desires their welfare would dare to inflict further suffering?"
He who inflicts suffering upon another certainly finds suffering himself;
therefore, O one who fears suffering, you must not give suffering to anyone.
Now, the specific vessels for giving are described.
Yama says: "He who bestows gold, silver, or copper upon ascetics does not obtain the fruit thereof; it merely returns to that very place."

‘Parivartaḥ’ means reversal; ‘evaśabdaḥ’ has the sense of ‘even’ (api). Therefore, ‘therein’—even in that which is fit to be given—it undergoes reversal, meaning it produces a result contrary to dharma.
As it has been said: “By giving gold to an ascetic, even the donor may go to hell.”

Devala says: One who desires merit should not give cooked food to a householder, nor milk products to a forest-dweller; these are the means of subsistence for those respective modes of life, and should not be given away by one seeking religious merit.
Likewise:
there is no "sustenance" (vṛtti)— meaning a livelihood beyond begging— from a Śūdra.
One should not offer sacrificial oblations to a Śūdra; however, one may accept from him curd, sesame seeds, and honey,
provided that these have been offered to others first.
Gold, a field, cows, sesame seeds, honey, and clarified butter—
as well as all men— must not be given even to Caṇḍālas.
Cēmādri. [[page 85-to-85]]
[Chapter 3 of the Dānakhaṇḍa:

Regarding the phrase "one should not say *svasti* to him," the meaning is that one should not utter the word *svasti* to a Śūdra without a prostration. Regarding the phrase "of them," it refers to other goods offered for sale by thieves and the like.]
This is the meaning.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not give to Śūdras kṛśara, pāyasa, barley-gruel, curd, honey, black antelope skins, or anything prepared by fire."
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: One should not give land, a cow, a horse, jewels, gold, sesame seeds, or an elephant without first ascertaining their merits and defects.
Now, that which may be accepted is stated.
Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"For the sake of one's family, one may accept what is unasked from a virtuous Śūdra."
One should never beg for the sake of one's livelihood or even for oneself.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: When a terrible famine has arrived and the family is perishing from hunger, one may, without lethargy, accept a gift even from an unrighteous person.
The best of the twice-born may accept gifts for the purpose of discharging a debt,
with the desire to perform a sacrifice, or for the sake of their mother and father.
One should always accept what is given with faith and purity from a Brāhmaṇa who constantly follows the path of right conduct; in this way, one's dharma does not decline.
Even from a gift made by one who is not a Brahmin, though it be entirely pure in every respect,
a Brahmin who knows the law should accept it, even if it is forbidden.

"Even that which is forbidden (*niṣiddham api*)," such as a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and so forth, [is permitted] when there is no distress (*anāpadi*). From the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "In times of distress, by accepting gifts from a sacrificer or a pupil according to the rule of extreme necessity (*atidharma*), a Brahmin does not fall away from his dharma."

For the sake of dharma, one should maintain a household in a manner that can be sustained for six months, one month, six days, three days, or even a single day, each subsequent mode being superior to the former.
The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter:
Hemādri.
From the Gāruḍa Purāṇa: A householder should indeed accept only so much as is sufficient to enable him to perform the five great sacrifices for himself and his family.
That gift which is received from blameless persons and is purified by faith certainly delivers the recipient.
Even a vast heap of wealth is better when received from one who is blameless;
however, even a tiny fragment of wealth from a blameworthy person leads only to hell.
Bṛhaspati says: Even from kings who have committed evil deeds, the virtuous accept gifts;
they desire nothing else, for this is the supreme means of purification.

From the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: For the sake of one's father, mother, and guru, for the purpose of marriage, and for the sake of sacrifice, a learned man should always accept wealth in accordance with dharma.
One should not hesitate in this way when accepting cattle, land, gold, and so forth;
rather, that which has been prepared should be accepted, provided it has been thoroughly examined many times.
The householder, ever disciplined, should constantly reflect upon dharma alone;
for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of those dependent on him, the wise man should desire wealth.
Even for one who has committed evil deeds, food brought unasked should be accepted;
likewise [the following].
Except for unchaste women, eunuchs, outcasts, and likewise enemies.
Yājñavalkya: A king may take from his pupils, dependents, and sacrificial clients what is necessary for the relief of hunger;
however, he should avoid those who are hypocrites, those motivated by deceit, heretics, and those who act like herons.
Likewise: For the sake of the gods, guests, the forest-dwellers, and for the support of teachers, dependents, and others, he may accept gifts from anyone whatsoever, and also for his own subsistence.

"From all sources" means even from a Śūdra and others. "Self-sustenance" refers merely to the maintenance of the body, not to satiety. Thus Viṣṇu says: "Desiring to support his gurus and dependents, and wishing to offer oblations to the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from all sources; however, he himself should not become satiated thereby."
56. Hemādri. [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3]
Aṅgiras said: For the sake of his teacher, guests, or especially his dependents, he may accept food from a Śūdra, but he must not eat it himself.
Manu says: Prajāpati considered that alms offered spontaneously, with the hands raised and before one has been asked, should be accepted even from a man of evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, he who treats those two with contempt.
Yājñavalkya: Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, a funeral pyre, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water—these should not be refused.
Manu says: Likewise—
bedding, houses, kusha grass, perfumes, water, flowers, earth, and curd.
One should not greedily snatch away fish, parched grain, milk, meat, or even vegetables.
One may accept from anyone fuel-wood, water, roots, fruits, whatever is offered spontaneously, honey, and the gift of safety.
"Fuel" means wood. "Offered" means that which has come unasked.
Aṅgiras says: Grain found in a threshing floor or a field, water from a pond or a well, and even milk found in a cow-pen—these may be taken even by one who does not give.
One may accept cooked food from Brahmins; grain and cattle even from a Kṣatriya;
all kinds of grain from a Vaiśya; but nothing at all should be accepted from a Śūdra.
(This refers to the case of food that is unfit to be eaten by Brahmins and others.
But as for grain situated in a field, or in a threshing floor, or outside the house—
it is the opinion of Aṅgiras that it may be taken at all times even from Śūdras.
* There is a variant reading, "cāhatābhyudyatām.
1 Another reading is "na nirnaded iti.
[Chapter 3 of the Dānakhaṇḍa] Hemādri:
For these [materials] become pure through purificatory rites (saṃskāra); therefore, they are traditionally held to be pure.
Therefore, a gift should be accepted even during periods of death or childbirth.
The phrase "even in the intervals between deaths and births" refers to that specific context.
Raw meat, honey, water, parched grain, milk, as well as molasses and buttermilk—these may be accepted even from a Śūdra; there is no prohibition against them.
Vegetables, fish, meat, boiled rice, fried grains, roasted flour, sesame seeds, sugarcane, fruits, and oil-cakes may be accepted from anyone.
*Kantukāḥ* means maidens.

*Bṛhaspati* says: "During marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, as well as during internal periods of impurity due to death or birth, all that has been previously resolved upon may be accepted; no fault is proclaimed [in this]."
Gāṅga:
At the birth of a son, one should give jaggery, sesame seeds, and gold to a woman who has not been previously defiled.
There is no fault in accepting garments, cows, and grain.
Regarding this, some say it may be done on that very day;
thus says Pracetās: "There is no fault in accepting the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) consisting of bipeds, quadrupeds, grain, or female slaves from all those who are of the same lineage."
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "The gift of life should be accepted even from a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa. By living, one obtains everything; while alive, one performs dharma.
The body is the entirety of one's dharma; it must be protected with great effort."
Now, that which is not to be accepted is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A Brāhmaṇa should always accept gifts from a virtuous person for the sake of his livelihood;
however, he should avoid sheep, horses, jewels, elephants, sesame seeds, and iron."
One who accepts a black antelope skin or sesame seeds shall not become a man again;
nor one who accepts the bed, ornaments, or garments of the deceased.
58 Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3]
One shall be delivered from the hells by gifting a cow, sesame seeds, and land;
one shall likewise cross over even the repeated theft of the wealth of Brahmins.
But how will that which has been taken from the sick person and others be delivered?
"From the sick" means from one who is about to die. From the Vahni Purāṇa: "Elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, as well as the beds and seats of the deceased—"
And the twice-born man who has gone abroad in times of distress takes up a black antelope skin.
Likewise, O twice-born one, [one who eats] the terrible earth with its two openings and its mountains,
or food given at Kurukṣetra by a Caṇḍāla or an outcaste,
or at a monthly śrāddha or a new śrāddha, shall attain the state of a preta.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "One who takes up a deerskin, a bed of the deceased, and a two-faced horn in Kurukṣetra shall not become a man again."
In the Padma Purāṇa: "The gift of the Brahmāṇḍa and the gift of land must not be accepted by one person alone;
he who accepts them incurs sin, there is no doubt—it is equivalent to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa."
Regarding the phrase "the gift of land," this concerns the gift of gold and earth, which is included among the sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*).
Vasiṣṭha states: "Weapons, poison, or liquor are not to be accepted by a Brāhmaṇa."
Regarding the acceptance of alms, Manu says:
"One should avoid the food offered even by one who has extended it, if that person is a physician, an ungrateful man, a surgeon, a usurer, a eunuch, or an unchaste woman."
(The word *bhikṣām* [alms] is to be supplied as the remainder. "A physician" here means a quack.
"A eunuch" means a cowardly man. "An unchaste woman" means a wanton woman.
Yama says: One should avoid the food offered by a physician, a hunter, a dyer, a gambler, a eunuch, and a dancer.
[Chapter 3 of the Dānakhaṇḍa, Hemādri:
"Mṛgayu" means a hunter, one who kills deer.
Vasiṣṭha said: Even when offered, [the gift] is not accepted from a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a snarer, a eunuch, or an unchaste woman.
Some maintain that the two qualifiers, "of the physician" (*pūracikitsakasya*) and "of the hunter with the net" (*mṛgayoḥ pāśinaḥ*), should be applied respectively to *śatya* and *kṛtam*.
Viṣṇu: Even when capable of performing these duties, one should not accept gifts from unchaste women, eunuchs, outcasts, nor from an enemy.

"In these" means in the previously mentioned [activities] such as the worship of the Guru, the deity, and the lunar day (tithi). Manu says: "One should not seek wealth through worldly attachment nor by prohibited actions; nor when wealth is already present, nor from here and there."
Yājñavalkya says: One should not seek wealth that conflicts with Vedic study, nor from just anyone;
one should never find satisfaction in engaging in forbidden activities.
Likewise: "In receiving gifts, the butcher, the oil-presser, the liquor-seller, the prostitute, and the king are wicked;
each subsequent one is ten times worse than the preceding one."
A *sūnī* is one who possesses *sūna*, which is the slaughter of living beings; thus, he is a killer of living creatures.
A *cakrī* is an oil-presser. A *dhvajī* is a maker of liquor. Sambarta says:
"Accepting gifts from a king is terrible; it has the taste of honey but is like poison."
It is better to eat the flesh of one's own son than to accept a gift from a king.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: One who, deluded by greed for wealth, abandons a Brāhmaṇa, is consumed by the acceptance of gifts from a king and does not attain rebirth.
But one who, greedy for the bait of sensory objects, accepts gifts from a king,
will certainly fall here into the terrible Raurava hell.
* "In the absence of [such] conceptualizations," is an alternative reading.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3].
Trees scorched by a forest fire sprout again at the arrival of the rainy season.
Those who have been consumed by accepting gifts from kings never sprout again at any time.
Likewise: "The acceptance of gifts from a king is terrible, fierce, sinful, and fearsome; who would have the power to endure the horrific torments in hell?"
Likewise: "I, the Brahman-sage Gālava, formerly resided at Kurukṣetra; due to the deficiency caused by accepting horses as a gift, I took refuge in the womb of a mare."
One who is burnt by a forest fire grows again from water;
but he who is burnt by the acceptance of gifts does not grow, for he is dead.
Manu says: A mendicant should never beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for by begging thus, a sacrificer is born as a Caṇḍāla after death.
Those who, having acquired wealth from a Śūdra, maintain the Agnihotra fire—
O Brāhmaṇas, they are all censurable and condemned among those who discourse on the Veda.
Likewise: "One who accepts gold, land, a horse, a cow, grain, clothing, sesame seeds, or clarified butter without knowing [their true nature] becomes like ashes, just like wood."
But a twice-born man who is without austerity, unlearned, and fond of accepting gifts,
sinks along with that very person, like one in water using a boat made of stone.
Therefore, an ignorant person should fear receiving gifts from anyone whatsoever; for even by means of a very small gift, the ignorant man sinks like a cow stuck in the mud.
Yājñavalkya: One who is deficient in learning and austerity must not accept a gift;
by accepting one, he leads both the giver and himself downward.
And therefore, even by one devoid of knowledge and austerity who is perishing, [there is gain] through the possession of much gold and other wealth;
"therefore" (*tasmāt*) is an alternative reading found in some manuscripts.
Chapter 3 of the Dānakhaṇḍa:
Hemādri states that one should accept only a small amount of wealth sufficient merely for the maintenance of one's family, and not more.

In this regard, it is understood that there is an excessive attachment [to receiving gifts], as stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Even one who is capable of accepting gifts should avoid such occasions;
for by accepting gifts, the spiritual luster (*brahmatejas*) of Brahmins is destroyed."
Without understanding the rules and the dharma regarding the acceptance of gifts,
a wise man should not accept them, even if he is perishing from hunger.

"Ritual injunction (*vidhi*) is characterized by the method of mantras and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Yājñavalkya says: 'Even though capable of receiving gifts, he who does not accept them attains those eternal worlds that belong to those whose nature is to give.'"
Thus ends the determination of substance.
Now, the limb of giving known as "time" (kāla) is explained.
Regarding that, first is the auspicious time for merit (*puṇyakāla*).
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Time is eternal, all-pervading, and constant; its various states are born of causes."
Through specific characteristics such as the signs and so forth, he bestows the fruit of merit in the world.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: ten nimeṣas make one kāṣṭhā, and eight [kāṣṭhās] make one kalā.
Thirty kāṣṭhās, together with thirty kalās, constitute one muhūrta.
Thirty muhūrtas are indeed recorded as one day and night for human beings.
Twenty such days and nights constitute a fortnight, and two fortnights are called a month. Six of those months make a solstice (ayanam), and those two—southern and northern—are a year.
That constitutes a day and night of the gods; among them, the northern course [of the sun] is the day.
‘With eighteen’ means with eighteen [verses]. It is said:
“The rites for the gods are in the forenoon, and those for humans at midday.”

As for the statement that one should perform bathing, giving gifts, and so forth even at night during transits and similar occasions, that refers specifically to the southern and northern solstices (*dakṣiṇāyana* and *uttarāyaṇa*). Therefore, it has been said: "Excluding..."

Regarding the statement "Capricorn and Cancer": one should understand that those specific *nāḍīs* (periods) which are prescribed for the bestowal of knowledge and grace during the night apply to Capricorn and Cancer as well. As for the prohibition of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth at night, that restriction indeed remains in force for other *saṃkrāntis*.

Regarding the subtle periods of merit at the equinoxes and other times, Gālava says: "The sages know that there are six *muhūrtas* of merit at the equinox (*viṣuva*), six at the commencement of the *ṣaḍaśīti*, and likewise three at the *viṣṇupada*."
Bharadvāja states the result:
"Whatever gift is given during the Ṣaḍaśīti, and whatever gift is given during the two equinoxes (Viṣuva),
the end of the ocean may be seen, but its end is never found."

Gālava describes the most subtle auspicious times, such as Viṣṇupada and others: "Viṣṇupada occurs in a fixed zodiac sign; Ṣaḍaśītimukha is beneficial in both Libra and Aries; the equinox (viṣuva) occurs in Capricorn during the northern transit (dakṣāyana), and the winter solstice (saumyaka) occurs when the Sun is in Cancer."
The Chapter on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), the [Xth] Adhyāya. Hemādri:
This has been explained by the preceding verses.
This becomes manifest in a period of time equal to the degrees of precession (ayanāṃśaka);
otherwise, in another year, all the divisions and so forth mentioned in the Viṣṇupada and other systems [would apply].
When the sun is in the signs beginning with Capricorn and Cancer, and its solstices are directed southward and northward respectively,
then the transits (saṃkrānti) are said to be the Viṣṇupada and so forth, which are occasions for giving gifts.
The meaning is this: there are thirty degrees for each sign (*rāśi*); the sun consumes one degree per day.
In that regard, by as many degrees as it takes for the solstitial shift (*ayana-cyuti*) to occur, [that much is the duration].
The fall (*cyuti*) of the [periods] beginning with Viṣṇupada occurs by means of the future time of enjoyment (*bhogyakāla*) of the sun;
therefore, when the fall of the solstice (*ayana*) occurs after twelve [months], then ten days prior to the impending transit (*saṃkrānti*),
there is a period of merit (*puṇyakāla*), and for that purpose, it is for the sake of pacifying that [transit].

One should perform acts such as giving; this should be understood to apply even when [the time] is deficient or excessive. It is not only at the time of the transit of the sun that there is a meritorious period (puṇyakāla), but rather, at the transit of all planets into a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) or a zodiacal sign (rāśi), there occurs a meritorious period.
Thus it is stated in the Jyotiḥśāstra:

"At the transit of the sun, the constellations and zodiac signs [beginning from the one entered] are auspicious for one *nāḍī* and the subsequent sixteen *nāḍīs*. Likewise, for the moon, four *yugas* consisting of three earth-measures (*apala*) [of time] are declared by the sages to be auspicious as a single *nāḍī*."
The four nāḍīs and one pala belong to Mars; for Mercury, three nāḍīs joined with thirteen palas;
the six nāḍīs and seven palas belong to Jupiter; and for Venus, four nāḍīs and one pala.
The two nāḍīs known as Nāḍā, together with seven palas, are declared by Manīvara to be highly meritorious;
performing recitation, charity, and fire-offerings during the beginning and middle [of these times], one attains the abode of the Lord of the Gods.
The meaning of this is as follows:

When the Sun enters a zodiac sign or a lunar mansion, the auspicious time (*puṇyakāla*) consists of sixteen *ghaṭikās* before and after that entry. Likewise, when the Moon enters a zodiac sign or a lunar mansion, it is one *ghaṭikā* and thirty *palas*.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3] Thus, regarding the auspicious ghaṭikā—

Thirteen *ghaṭikās* and one *pala* after [the conjunction] is the auspicious time for Mercury (*puṇyakāka*). Likewise, for Mercury (*budha*), three *ghaṭikās* and fourteen *palas* is the auspicious time. For Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*) as well, it is four and a half *ghaṭikās*.
The auspicious time for Venus is seven palas; for Saturn as well, the auspicious time is four ghaṭikās and one pala.
"An auspicious time."
The Śautighaṭikā:
now, the miscellaneous times (prakīrṇakālāḥ).

Seven *pala*s [of gold] are for Viṣṇu on the day of a planetary conjunction (*graha*). The new moon (*amāvasyā*), the *vyatīpāta* yoga, an eclipse of the moon or sun, the beginnings of the Manvantaras and Yugas, the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), and likewise the *vaidhṛti* yoga [are occasions for such offerings].
The end of a day, a gap in the day, and likewise an omitted day (avama);
the two solstices, the two equinoxes, and the six seasonal transitions (ṣaḍayutimukha); the four Viṣṇupadas, and furthermore, the birth of a son and other such occasions.
When there is a conjunction of the planets, such as the Sun and others, with the lunar mansions (nakṣatras),
this auspicious time (puṇyakāla) is to be recognized by those learned in astrology after due deliberation;
one should perform acts such as giving charity therein for the sake of increasing one's own merit.
The new moon days (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth are well known. Regarding the "loss of a day" (*dinakṣaya*), it is stated in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"When two lunar day-ends (*tithyanta*) fall on a single weekday, that shall be a loss of a day.
Vasiṣṭha also said: "When there is a triad of lunar days within a single civil day (*sāvana*...)"
Then the destruction of the day is declared; your fruit shall be a thousandfold.

Bhṛgu states the definition of the "day-break" (dinacchidra): Bhārgava has declared that the first day of the lunar month (pratipad) when it falls on a Tiṣya (Puṣya) asterism, and the day of the new moon (śaśi-parvan), are both designated as "day-breaks."
This is the meaning: [Hemādri, in the section on gifts (Dānakhaṇḍa), chapter 3, page 108], this is the procedure for the lunar day (tithi), the Karaṇas, the Yogas, and the Nakṣatras.
At the beginning of the seventy-seven mantras and the parvan, the time is equal to a lunar eclipse, and it is designated as a "day-interval" (dinachidra).
The measurement of time has also been stated by that same [author]:
"The time for cutting and so forth is declared to be two ghaṭīs before the lunar day (tithi) begins."
It is endowed with the palas of the *nāgavahī* plant and joined with the palas of *tattva*.
Two nāḍīs joined with sixteen palas from the conjunction is declared to be the time for the *cheda* and other rites; when a gift is given during this period, it yields infinite fruit.
‘Kṛti’ means eight; ‘nāga’ means eight; ‘vakrayaḥ’ means three; ‘bha’ means a lunar mansion (nakṣatra);
‘tattva’ means twenty-five; and ‘yuti’ means conjunction (yoga). This is the meaning that results for the *sica*.
(For the lunar day and the karaṇa, the auspicious time consists of two ghaṭikās and thirty-eight palas at their beginning and end).
(For the lunar mansion, however, it consists of two ghaṭikās joined with twenty-five palas). (For the yoga as well, it consists of two ghaṭikās joined with sixteen palas).
Viṣṇu defines the characteristic of an *avamadina*: "When a single weekday touches three lunar days (*tithi*), that indeed is called an *avamadina*.
Since a lunar day touches three weekdays and also touches [the next] day, it is so designated."

(In this regard, there is this much difference between *dinacaya* and *avamadina*): where the end of the weekday coincides with the end of the lunar day (*tithi*), that is *dinacaya*; whereas where the end of the weekday occurs even before the end of the lunar day, that is *avamadina*.
As stated by Brahmā:
"The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), the new moon (Amāvāsyā), the full moon (Pūrṇimā), and the birth of a son."
The Vyatīpāta yoga, the Bhadrā tithi, and the day of the waning moon (the new moon).
The conjunctions of the planets, their respective nodes, those with equal longitudinal degrees, the equality of declination, the gaps in the days, and the planetary divisions (bhagas).
Cemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 2]
"Bhagama" means moving through the zodiac signs and lunar mansions.
As stated in the Devīpurāṇa: "Vyatīpāta, Viṣṇupada, and likewise Śar̤aśītimukha..."
The equality of declination, the new moon, eclipses, the Vaidhṛti yoga,
the solar transits (saṃkrānti), the "gaps" in the day (dinacchidra), the increase of lunar days (tithi-vṛddhi), and the decrease of days—
these and others are the auspicious times for rites such as fire-offerings (homa) and giving (dāna).
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "An eclipse of the moon or sun, the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*),

the equinox (*viṣuva*), the *vyatīpāta* yoga, as well as the *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, the 'gaps' of the day (*dinacchidra*), the *saṃkrānti*, and furthermore the *viṣṇupada*— these are to be known [as times for meritorious action]."
Thus has the time been described, which increases the merit of men;
gifts given during this period, as well as ritual baths, fire-offerings, and austerities,
shall yield infinite fruit and even bestow heaven and liberation.

Cyavana said: [The times for offering are] the new moon, the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), the vyatīpāta yoga, the equinoxes (viṣuva), the solstices (ayana), the commencement of the six signs (ṣaḍaśītimukha), and the Viṣṇu...
The period beginning from the footstep until the grasping [of the vessel] is that very time of merit.
During the solstices, during the sixty-fourth [day], likewise during lunar and solar eclipses, at the beginning of the Yugas, and during the Viṣṭi yoga, what is given becomes inexhaustible.
Śātātapa said: "That which is given during the solstices (ayanāni), at the beginnings of the six periods of increase (ṣaḍaśītimukhāni),
and during lunar and solar eclipses, becomes inexhaustible."
Nārada said: When the sun is in Viśākhā and the moon is in Kṛttikā, that conjunction is named Padmaka; it is extremely difficult to obtain at Puṣkara.
Now, the times for the twilight rituals (*niṣicakāla*). Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One should avoid food, sexual intercourse, and sleep during the time of the twilights."
Chapter 2 of the Dānakhaṇḍa: Hemādri states that [these are] ritual action, Vedic study, as well as giving and receiving gifts.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "A gift should never be given by anyone at night;
because Rākṣasas seize it, it brings fear to the donor."
Especially at midnight, a virtuous deed does not lead to well-being;
therefore, a wise person should avoid the middle of the night for acts such as giving.
Likewise, upon the death of a preceptor (mahāguru), one should not perform ritual bathing, great gifts, Vedic recitation,
or libations during the first year.

Jyotiḥparāśara said: One should avoid the establishment of the sacred fires, the consecration of temples, sacrifices, acts of charity and the undertaking of vows, auspicious ceremonies, and royal ablutions during an intercalary month (malamāsa).
When performing the consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, one should face the north during the sun's northern course;
if one performs it facing the southern direction, one shall not obtain the fruit thereof.
Whether it be for a child or an elder, or even when Indra has set [in the form of a solar eclipse],
one should always diligently avoid these [rites] during an intercalary month.

"Intercalary month" (*malamāsa*) refers to the *adhikamāsa*. Its definition is stated by Pracetas: "When two new moon days (*darśa*) occur while the sun remains in a single zodiac sign (*rāśi*), that [second month] should be known as the intercalary month (*adhimāsaka*), which destroys the performance of rites for the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*)."

Paiṭhīnasi says: "The intercalary month (*adhimāsaka*), which occurs within the year and is not a true transit (*asaṃkrānta*), is a sinful period that destroys the fruit of sacrifices; it belongs to the Nairṛtas and the Yātudhānas."
One should recognize the *adhimāsa* (intercalary month) as that which lacks the *malimbuca* transit and is devoid of the sun's transit; it is censured in all ritual activities.

Likewise: "All rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti are declared to be performed in the twelfth month;
however, in the thirteenth month, all of them are designated as fruitless."
Therefore, one should not perform those [rites] in the thirteenth month under any circumstances;
by performing them, one would quickly bring about only misfortune and the destruction of oneself.
Hārīta says:
That month is proclaimed as the beginning [of the year] in which Indra and Agni are offered;
Agni and Soma are in the middle; and Pitṛsoma are at the conclusion.
But when the sun ever passes beyond [the limit],
it should be known as the first *mālinīcchanda*, while the second is remembered as the *prākṛta*.
In that same ordinary month, one should perform the śrāddha according to the rules;
likewise, an auspicious rite (abhyudaya) should always be performed once at all times.
Vyāsa says: A month is eclipsed by the sun in all ritual acts;
a month is said by the sons of Vadarāyaṇa to consist of sixty days.
Having abandoned the first half, the latter half is praised.

The Upākarma rite, the offerings to the gods (havya), the offerings to the ancestors (kavya), as well as the seasonal festivals and celebrations—these one should perform during the latter part [of the lunar day]; if performed during the former part, they become fruitless.

Pārāśara says: The commencement of Vedic study (*upākarma*), as well as its conclusion (*utsarga*), the festivals marking the passing of the months, the *iṣṭakā* offerings, and the ancestral rites (*paitṛka*)—these should be performed after the full moon day, except for the ancestral rites themselves.
Likewise, in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra):
"When the sun has entered the signs of Aquarius, Virgo, Scorpio,
Sagittarius, Capricorn, or Aquarius, an intercalary month (adhimāsa) is not prescribed."
Māṇḍavya says: [The impurity lasts] for a fetus, for one who died of usury, for a ghost, and for the daily and monthly [śrāddhas].
There is an alternative reading: "pramavāco'kādayaḥ."

81. Now, it is stated that even for that which is prohibited, there is a period of merit (puṇyakāla) due to specific circumstances.
Devala says: "At the sight of Rāhu [an eclipse], at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), at marriages, deaths, and during rains..."
Bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts should not be performed at night, nor during optional religious observances (kāmya-vratas).
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: "During eclipses, weddings, transits [of the sun], journeys, and the birth of a child, giving is to be known as occasional (naimittika); it is desired even at night."

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "In this context, there is the worship of guests and even of travelers; that should be understood as taking place at night, and likewise the worship of cows has been prescribed."
In the Mahābhārata, they praise giving at night— except for the gift of fearlessness,
knowledge, a maiden, O best of the twice-born, a lamp, and shelter here.
In the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"The 'Great Night' (mahāniśā) should be understood as the two middle praharas;
one should not perform a bath there, except for that which is performed for specific desires or on specific occasions."
Viśvāmitra says: O Ghaṭikā, during the deep night, that is, in the two middle watches of the night, one may perform occasional rites (naimittika), but not even the slightest regular (nitya) rite.
Furthermore, by virtue of following the auspicious signs, all times are always occasions for merit.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Every time is prescribed and every recipient is declared suitable;
however, in the granting of fearlessness, no deliberation need be made.
That alone is the time for giving when danger has arisen."
No restriction of time is seen regarding the granting of shelter;
its gift is perfected at that very moment when the arrival of the traveler occurs.
For one should not wait for the right time to give water to one who is afflicted by thirst; likewise,
[one should give] whenever a worthy recipient arrives.
Hemādri: [Chapter 3 of the Dānakhaṇḍa] | "Water should always be given," so said the blessed Manu.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: One should give a cow that has just calved, without considering the time or other factors;
for that very moment is the auspicious time for the acceptance [of the gift], when the cow’s face is turned toward the moon.
Vyāsa says:
A cow with her calf should be given by one whose death is imminent, as previously described;
in its absence, a cow alone is indeed for the warding off of hell.
If at that time one is unable to give the Vaitaraṇī cow,
then another capable person, having given it, should provide for his welfare by giving the Amṛta cow as well.

In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "The Vyatīpāta yoga, the Saṃkrānti (the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign), and likewise an eclipse of the sun—all these are meritorious times when death has arrived. At such a time, the gift of cows, land, gold, and so forth, becomes inexhaustible."
Likewise: "O King, as long as the umbilical cord has not been severed once the son is born, they say that period is equal to an eclipse of the moon or the sun."

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O best of the twice-born, that which is given when the umbilical cord has not yet been severed upon the birth of a son, as well as during the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) of the son, is proclaimed to be inexhaustible."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Whenever wealth arises accompanied by a mind endowed with faith, that very moment is the time for giving, for life is indeed impermanent."
Thus concludes the determination of time.
Now, the factor of giving known as "place" (deśa) is being introduced.
In that regard, the Devīpurāṇa states: "All hermitages of Śiva are meritorious, and all rivers bestow auspiciousness;
they constantly grant men the fruits of giving, ritual bathing, fasting, and other such acts."
Viṣṇu said: "That country in which the established order of the four castes does not exist should be known as a Mleccha country; other than that is the Ārya country."
