Hemādri:
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, it is said: "Where [the merit] does not diminish..."
O twice-born one, that entire land, consisting of four quarters, is my supreme and eternal abode, most meritorious in every respect.
O best of Brahmins, that region where the practice enjoined by the scriptures is observed is considered supreme.
Yājñavalkya: In that land where the deer is black, there you should understand the Dharma.
In the Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: That region which lies to the north of the Sahya mountain, where the river Godāvarī flows— that area is the most purifying on the entire earth.
Vyāsa says: At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at Avimukta and Puṣkara;
at the city of Aṭṭahāsa, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean;
at Kurukṣetra, at Gayā, and at the sacred site of Amarakaṇṭaka.
What is given at such sacred fords as these becomes inexhaustible; for the Gaṅgā embodies all sacred fords, and what is given there yields great fruit.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, the Puṣkara lakes,
the banks of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Naimiṣa, Amarakaṇṭaka,
Śrīparvata, Mahākāla, Gokarṇa, and Vedaparvata.
These and other regions, frequented by gods and sages, have been thus described.

All mountains are meritorious, as are all rivers together with the oceans; and those regions where cows, perfected beings (siddhas), and sages dwell are proclaimed to be meritorious. Whatever is given at these sacred fords (tīrthas) shall produce infinite fruit.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "Wherever the Gaṅgā flows facing north and the Sarasvatī flows eastward, there the merit of bathing and giving gifts is equal to that of a hundred sacrifices."
Whether it be a *liṅga* or even an image, wherever it may be seen;
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3] All that attains merit and yields great fruit among gifts.
It is declared by Brahmā that a gift given on a riverbank, in a cow-pen, or in the house of Brāhmaṇas is said to be a hundredfold,
while one given in the presence of the Sun is a hundred-thousandfold.
What is given in the presence of Śiva, Viṣṇu, or Brahmā becomes inexhaustible;
likewise, [what is given] at the Agnihotra sacrifice, in a cow-pen, or in a place purified by the sound of the Vedas.
Whatever is given, even if it be small, at a site dedicated to Śiva,
should be known as yielding infinite fruit due to the power of the sacred field of Śiva.
In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "O Earth, wherever a stone originating from Śālagrāma, adorned with the marks of a discus,
stands, that very place extends for three *yojanas*."
O Goddess, the stone from Dvāravatī is sealed with my seal;
wherever it is taken, that place shall become a sacred ford extending twelve yojanas.
Likewise: "By giving at sacred fords such as Prayāga, in holy shrines, and in rivers and sacred groves, one obtains inexhaustible merit."
"Āyatana" refers to a sacred field such as that of Śaṅkara. As it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"The field of Śiva, the Supreme Self, extends for the distance of one *krośa*."
The death of living beings there is said to be the cause for attaining union with Śiva;
and the fruit of offerings made there is proclaimed to be infinite.
This measurement of the field is prescribed when the lines are established by human beings;
in the case of a self-manifested (svayambhu) image, it should be one thousand [units], and in the case of a work of the sages (ārṣa), half of that.
Now, the factor of giving known as faith is described in the Skanda Purāṇa: "One should bestow a gift with diligence, purified by hearing [the sacred teachings], and free from sloth."
Those who listen [to the Dharma] enjoy the infinity of even a very small gift.
Chapter 3: The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa) [pages 116–116]
Hemādri says:
Even if one gives away one's entire possessions, O best of men, that does not lead to fruit; therefore, one should take refuge in the *Cāmuṇḍā*.
Devala says: By giving even a handful of vegetables with faith and devotion to a great person who is a worthy recipient, one shall attain all prosperity.
In the Mahābhārata: "That dharma which is accomplished by the great through vast heaps of wealth—munis who possess nothing, yet are full of faith, have gone to heaven."
Faith is the supreme cause of wealth, worldly pleasure, and liberation;
for those men who lack faith, there is neither dharma nor its fruit.
From the Vahnipurāṇa: All dharmas are preceded by faith (śraddhā), have faith as their middle, and are established in faith;
indeed, it is proclaimed that faith alone is the foundation of all dharmas.
The subtle Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara, whose essence consists solely of being heard, are apprehended by hearing alone;
they are not grasped by a sentence, nor by the eye.
The subtle Dharma is not attained through many bodily hardships nor by heaps of wealth, even by the gods who are devoid of faith.
Faith is the supreme, subtle Dharma; faith is knowledge, and austerity is destroyed without it. Faith is heaven and liberation; indeed, faith is this entire world.
Even if one were to give away all one's possessions and even one's life out of faith, yet if one does not obtain anything at all, one should therefore become one who possesses faith.
Vedavyāsa said: O King, Śraddhā is indeed the virtuous goddess, the daughter of the Sun;
she is the progenitress, the bringer-forth, and likewise the one who inspires confidence in all living beings.
Through Śraddhā, O Bhārata, speech is made eloquent and the mind is matured.

In the Mahābhārata: "One who performs ritual actions, possesses faith, is charitable, wise, free from malice, and discerns the distinctions between dharma and adharma, crosses over everything that is difficult to cross."
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 3] "The Śruti is like a mother, the progenitor of both knowledge and merit;
therefore, having produced knowledge by hearing it, one should acquire merit."
Manu says: One should always perform sacrifices and works of public utility with great effort;
for when performed with wealth acquired through righteous means, these two become inexhaustible.
Yājñavalkya says: One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on specific occasions;
even when solicited, one should give according to one's ability, provided it is pure and free from debt.

Bṛhaspati says: "If there should be a defect in the mantra or the clarified butter, or a deficiency in the austerity or the sensory faculties, or if there should be some deficiency in the portioning of the offering, it may at times become improperly performed."
Furthermore, this determination of the place has already been explained in detail in the *Bratakhaṇḍa* and other sections;

here, however, only the essential knowledge is presented for the purpose of fulfilling the promise to determine the five factors of the act of giving (*dāna*), such as the recipient (*pātra*). Nor is it the case that here, according to the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*, the five factors of giving are not determined.
One might suspect: "If [the donor] is being mentioned, why is the donor—who is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the act of giving—not mentioned separately?
This should not be suspected, because giving is impossible apart from the donor; thus, the donor is implied by the very act of giving itself.
If that were the case, then place, time, and so forth would likewise not be mentioned.

Thus one acts. "May you, sirs, declare it an auspicious day! "Śrīm! It is an auspicious day!"

For our well-being we invoke Vāyu at the rising and at the setting of the sun; may Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all things, grant us well-being; may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are uninjured, grant us well-being;
may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.

The eight gods, the Vasus, who are worthy of Soma; the four goddesses, most renowned through their radiance—may they protect the sacrifice from the east of the mid-region. May the year grant me immortality and well-being.
May you all pronounce blessings!

Long life to you! May we prosper; may we accomplish our hymn of praise and all success. Having approached with oblations and salutations, may we increase the god Mitra, the friend who bestows friendship. Increasing him with the *anūrādha* offering, may we live for a hundred autumns, possessing wealth. Three by three are the offerings to the gods; three indeed.
There are three pressings; these are the three worlds. He thus establishes himself in these worlds. "May you say 'it has prospered'! [He says:
"Born for glory, for the sake of glory, in whom the sacred word (brahman) conquered all this—both that world and this world—all that was here. In that regard, he releases it.
Hemādri, Chapter 3 of the Dānakhaṇḍa, page 180.

May the *kṣatra* be victorious; may it bestow glory upon me while being won. O unerring one, protect this mantra for me, which the seers who know the three Vedas know: the *yajus*, the *ṛc*s, the *sāmans*, and the *yajūṃṣi*.
May prosperity not fail; "May there be prosperity," let your honors say. Prosperity has been attained; it is an auspicious day.
"May there be prosperity; may the Blessed Lord Prajāpati be pleased.
Thus ends [the work] composed by Śrī Hemādri—the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the sovereign of all Karṇāṭas, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
The Section on General Explanations in the Chapter on Gifts within the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*.
The Fourth Chapter:
Now, the fruits of giving.
Having rendered his birth desirable through his conduct within the lineage of the twice-born, [he...]
By means of various collections of virtues, he fashioned for his fame a path that rises above all others;
by means of the Mīmāṃsā, he grasped that certain supreme light, through which the greatness of giving— which yields lofty fruits— is illustrated as if it were his own self.
That Hemādri, who always praises Śiva as proclaimed in all the scriptures on gifts,
today declares the fruit of giving as proclaimed in all the scriptures on gifts.
In that regard, in the Sāmaveda Upaniṣad:

"Through giving, one obtains all desires; by practicing celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one is born long-lived, handsome, and non-violent; through the offering of oblations (*paṇīśana*), one attains heaven and becomes a celestial being who moves upon the earth."
"One who possesses steadfastness, heroism, and self-control, who is devoted to the service of father, mother, and teacher, and who practices meditation, attains heaven through the gift of gold.
Thus spoke the Blessed Ṛgveda.

"High in heaven have those who give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) ascended; those who give horses dwell with the sun. Those who give gold partake in immortality; those who give garments, O Soma, prolong their lifespan."—thus says Hārīta. By giving water, one overcomes thirst and redeems oneself by means of a niṣka coin.
And in some places, the reading is "maṇīgatāt.
[Page 182] Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 4: Hemādri.
From not giving breath,
one becomes breathless; he expels it.

By giving food, one becomes possessed of food, an eater of food, and a lord of food; by the gift of clothing, one casts off old skin; by being well-formed and possessing fire, one becomes a possessor of clothing.
By the gift of gold, one ransoms his vital luster; being highly resplendent and glorious, he becomes a partaker of gold.
By the gift of a cow, one ransoms his speech; being eloquent and free from sin, he becomes a partaker of cows.
By the gift of an ox, one ransoms his vital breaths; being free from disease, strong, and capable of bearing the yoke, he becomes a partaker of oxen.

And he becomes a partaker [of rewards]: by the gift of a chariot, he ransoms his body and becomes a partaker of various celestial palaces for his servants; by the gift of a bed, he departs in comfort and becomes a partaker of the various splendors of happiness consisting of vehicles, beds, and seats.
Through giving immeasurably, one nourishes immeasurable merit and attains immeasurable desires.
That [giving] is of two kinds: giving that is unrecognized and giving that is recognized.

That which one gives to a learned man who does not know [the ritual] is a gift known [only as such]; but that which one gives and receives from a learned fellow-student (*sabrahmacārin*) who knows [the ritual] and is receiving the *vaiśvānara* [oblation], that is a "known gift" (*vijñāta-dāna*).
This too is stated in the *Yajus*: "To whom did he give this? (ŚB 12.4.1.4).

"He offers himself" (niṣkoṇati) means that he gives himself alone; by this method, the giving of water and so forth is indeed praised. Viṣṇu: "By the gift of vessels made of precious metals, one becomes a vessel for [the fulfillment of] desires."

Through the gift of honey, ghee, and oil, one gains health; through the gift of medicine, [health]; through the gift of salt, beauty; through the gift of grain, contentment; likewise through the gift of crops; through the gift of fuel, one's fire becomes bright and one attains readiness in battle; and through the gift of a seat, a place.

By the gift of a bed one obtains a wife; by the gift of sandals, a chariot yoked with mules; by the gift of land, heaven; by the gift of a palm-leaf fan or a fly-whisk, freedom from suffering; by the gift of flowers, one becomes superior; and by the gift of ointment, one becomes possessed of fame.
152 Hemādri.
[Chapter 4 of the Section on Giving] Manu said: "The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, inexhaustible happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, excellent vision."
The giver of land attains long life; the giver of gold, [great] strength;
the giver of a house, excellent dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
On the left, [he beholds] the lunar realm, the realm of the Aśvins, and the giver of horses;
the giver of oxen [beholds] abundant prosperity, and the giver of cows [beholds] the world of Viṣṇu.
The giver of vehicles and beds obtains a wife; the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty;
the giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and the giver of the Veda attains equality with Brahman.
"Brahmasārṣṭitām" means having a state equal to that of Brahmā.
[Thus said] Yājñavalkya: Land, lamps, horses, food, clothing, water, sesame seeds, silver, and shelter.
Having provided one's own draft animals for lodging, one is glorified in heaven.
By giving a house, grain, fearlessness, sandals, an umbrella, garlands, and ointments,
as well as a vehicle, a tree, prosperity, and a bed, one shall become supremely happy.
‘Pratiśrayaḥ’ is a shelter for travelers.
‘Naiveśikam’ is wealth intended for the purpose of marriage.
[Also included are: massaging those who are weary, attending to the sick, and the worship of the gods.
Washing the feet and clearing away the remnants of a twice-born person's meal are equal to the gift of a cow.
Having given shelter in this world, and likewise having granted the gift of fearlessness through one's word,
and similarly having provided a funeral pyre for a Brahmin, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The giver of a house attains a palace, and likewise, the giver of a city;
similarly, by the gift of sandals, one obtains an unsurpassed chariot.
By the offering of fuel, a blazing fire is produced upon the earth;
by the offering of morsels of grass to cows, one is liberated from all sins.
Hemādri, Chapter 4 of the Dānakhaṇḍa:
The giver of gold obtains everything; the giver of silver obtains excellent beauty.
One who gives a horse attains the same world as the Moon by beholding it, and the same world as the Sun.
Having given royal regalia and various jewels,
and likewise having given a city, one becomes a king upon the earth.
Likewise: removing the garlands from the gods, clearing the temples of the gods, performing the *acana* (worship) for Brahmins, and removing the distress of the twice-born.
Having prepared the washing of the feet, she should provide service,
as well as the application of oil to the feet and the massaging of one who is fatigued.
Scratching the backs of cows, the honoring and greeting of villages,
the giving of alms and lamps, and likewise the worship of guests.
Yama has declared that the merit of each of these is equal to the gift of a cow for one who,
having gathered together the necessary materials, bestows them upon Brahmins.
I am not able to describe his worlds earned through merit.
One should always remain filled with joy after giving to the Brahmins the materials for sacrificial and matrimonial rites, as well as fruits, roots, drinks, various kinds of vegetables, and vehicles.
Likewise: "One who gives grain and water enjoys happiness for six months;
one should give sandals, umbrellas, and seats to the Brahmins."
And by giving various kinds of gifts, one becomes a king;
likewise, by giving food, one becomes handsome, well-satisfied, and also possessed of fame.
A man who gives oil, āmalaka fruit, and likewise foot-massage,
becomes radiant and happy even while asleep.
154 Hemādri. [[page 185-to-185]]
[The Section on Giving,
Chapter 4] Likewise: "By giving earth, cow-dung, *darbha* grass, and a sacred thread (*upavīta*) to a virtuous Brahmin, one shall be born into an excellent family."
He who gives a comfortable dwelling as well as a tooth-cleansing stick shall become pure, fortunate, eloquent, and always happy.
He who provides a Brahmin with the purification of the feet, as well as the purification of the anus and the genitals, shall always remain pure and free from affliction.
He who gives fragrant herbs, anointing oil, honey, and likewise salt to a Brahmin, obtains good fortune.
Atri says: He who gives food during a famine, gold during times of plenty, and water in the wilderness, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Devala says: One who does not withhold what has been promised ascends to heaven by means of a celestial chariot;
one who provides medical treatment for the sick obtains the merit of giving away ten cows.
By washing the feet of a Brahmin, one obtains the fruit born of the gift of a cow;
by giving sandalwood, a palm-leaf fan, fruits, flowers, betel-leaf, a seat, and a bed, one shall become exceedingly happy.

Kātyāyana says: They should be especially honored by the best of the twice-born with foot-massage, head-anointing, gifts, honors, worship, and other such acts, as well as with particularly pleasant words.
In the *Yuga-purāṇa*: "Those who give gifts of sandalwood, conch shells, and pearls rescue their ancestors—even those who have committed sins—according to the sacred tradition."
In the Bhārata: "By giving a female slave, a male slave as an ornament, fields, houses,
and a daughter as a brahmadeya gift, one attains heaven without a doubt."
And the man who offers oblations and flowers attains the auspicious state;
"bhogipratikriya" is an alternative reading.
Likewise, in the fourth chapter of the Dānakhaṇḍa, Hemādri states:
"By the gift of draft-oxen and likewise by horses, a man attains the worlds of Vaśanā."
By the gift of an umbrella one obtains an excellent house, and likewise by the gift of sandals, a vehicle.

By the gift of clothing, one gains a beautiful form; by the gift of perfume, a man becomes fragrant. By giving food, drink, and flavors to a mendicant, one obtains all flavors to one's heart's content.
The man who provides shelter and clothing obtains those very things; there is no doubt in this matter.
Furthermore, the man who gives garlands, incense, perfumes, ointments, baths, and flower wreaths to the twice-born shall become free from disease and handsome in the world of kings.
Likewise, he who bestows sandalwood, agallochum, and incense upon the Brahmins,
as well as betel-leaf and garlands, shall become a lord who proceeds to heaven.
Giving sesame seeds, water, a lamp, mantras, and shelter,
as well as these truthful words, are for the virtuous who desire heaven.
One who bestows consolation attains everything and is liberated from all sorrows.
By the gift of spectacles, one obtains memory and intelligence.

In the Āditya Purāṇa: "Those who are givers of the treatises on Dharma, those who delight in the giving of sacrificial sessions (satras), and those who provide boats, bridges, and the like at holy fords, tanks, wells, and so forth."
He who provides water for those afflicted by thirst carries them across on his own shoulder;
he who gives irrigated fields yields ripe grain, and he who gives fruit-bearing trees yields abundant fruit.
Sixty thousand crores and three arbudas of them indeed sport in the city of heaven; this, O best of the twice-born, has been told to you.
Whether it be a horse, or a draft animal, or beautiful sandals— whosoever, being well-restrained, gives such a gift to Brahmins;
For him, there shall be divine vehicles— chariots adorned with banners and flags—
and no evil path whatsoever shall exist here for him in any way.
Likewise:
156 Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 4].
Herein [are mentioned] drinks, horses, cows, garments, umbrellas, beds, and seats.
In the world of the hungry ghosts (preta), eight types of gifts are especially praised.
In the Liṅgapurāṇa: "Having given clothing, water, and a sacred thread to a Śiva-yogin, one attains great enjoyment and, in the end, eternal yoga."
He who gives a seat, a bed, or a vehicle to one who is illustrious,
being impartial toward all beings, for him no suffering exists.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Every single day, one should offer anointing oil, fuel, water, as well as a bed and a seat, and likewise food for the daily rites, dedicated to him."
One should offer a bodily gift of mantra dedicated to that [deity];
or rather, what is the use of much talk—whatever meritorious deed is performed on this earth [should be offered].
Performing [these acts] with devotion directed toward Śiva, one attains that state effortlessly.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Substances such as land, gold, cows, grain, sesame seeds, clothing, clarified butter, and so forth..."
By means of ritual, fasting, eating only once a day, eating only at night,
being pure, purified in heart, and through self-restraint, truthfulness, vows, and so forth.

Even one who gives as little as a mustard seed shall be delivered by that act of giving. In the *Āditya Purāṇa* it is said: "Furthermore, Keśava becomes pleased by the gift of land and the gift of food."
The Moon becomes pleased by offerings of molasses, milk, ghee, and garments; Varuṇa is always well-pleased by the gift of water;
and Maheśvara shall be gratified by the gift of silver.
By the gift of gold, Agni is eternally pleased;
likewise, by the gift of elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and seats, Indra is gratified.
By means of beds, houses, the Dharma-sūtras, and even the sun,
Yama brought about the arrival of the bull of the Kapardin with his rays.
By the gift of two sandals, the Lotus-born (Brahmā) is highly pleased. *Hemādri*, *Dānakhaṇḍa*, Chapter 4. [[page 188-to-188]]
And Pārvatī, the mother of the world, was likewise honored with ornaments and marks of respect.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: He who gives a cow that is well-adorned, yielding milk, and provided with bell-metal vessels, clothing, and so forth, as well as a buffalo, obtains all his desires.
In the Saura Purāṇa: "A black antelope skin, a buffalo, two rams, ten cows, and the Tulāpuruṣa [gift] indeed bestow the world of Brahmā."
In the Vahni Purāṇa: "O Sage, for those who always delight in giving vehicles, horses, elephants, gold, silver, gems, and sesame seeds to the sinless,
the path of Bhairava never arises."
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, Haṃsa said:
"O best of Brahmins, by the gift of a seat, a man finds a place everywhere; and by the gift of a bed, he obtains a wife."
By giving a well-spread bed with an upper cover to a twice-born man,
one attains birth in a great family, endowed with beauty and wealth.
In that same way, he obtains a wife who is submissive to his will;
by this very act of giving, a wife likewise obtains her husband.
By the gift of a canopy, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, O Brahmins, there is no need for deliberation regarding the gift of an umbrella.
Having seen the parasol with its hundred ribs that wards off the heat from the sight,
one who is liberated from all sins is glorified in the heavenly world.
O best of the twice-born,
by giving a pair of sandals imbued with oil to a dog, one likewise proceeds easily along the path of Yama.
One attains the third heaven in a chariot yoked with female mules.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 4] "Completely liberated from all sins, one shall travel easily along the path of Yama."
By the gift of a palm-leaf fan, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, by the gift of a chowrie, one is freed from all sufferings;
and by the gift of sandals, one attains an auspicious state.
By the gift of a footstool, one finds a place everywhere;
likewise, by giving a staff to a twice-born man, one attains a secure station.
By the gift of a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), one obtains the fruit of the gift of clothing;
likewise, this is declared to be the fruit of the gift of a turban (uṣṇīṣa).
By the gift of a tooth-stick, one shall obtain great good fortune;
by the gift of clay, one becomes pure in all circumstances.
By giving water for cleansing and bathing, one is born free from disease;
likewise, one who always provides oil for anointing attains the destruction of illness.
Likewise, by the gift of medicine, one hears of the destruction of disease;
and by giving fragrant substances brought from one's own home, one attains good fortune.
By the gift of ointments, one is born beautiful;
likewise, one attains the radiance of bodily fire, clarity, and the highest state.
But he who gives [land] to a Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of performing a sacrificial rite goes to the same world as Agni and attains the destruction of his enemies.
Having given metallic vessels together with salt,
one who bestows metallic vessels containing oil [obtains great merit].

Supreme health is proclaimed, as is supreme beauty. Likewise, one who gives vessels produced from the ocean, such as conch shells and the like, becomes a recipient of all desires and of fame; of this there is no doubt.
The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 8:
Hemādri.
Likewise,
by giving to one who is in need, one releases oneself from supreme affliction.
The gift of a bed brings about the highest status in the worlds;
likewise, by giving ointment and garlands, one attains supreme prosperity.
O best of the twice-born, it is said that he who properly offers a man as a vehicle for you obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By the gift of a palanquin, one obtains the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice;
he who provides a warrior goes to the same world as Śakra.
For him who bestows laborers and servants upon a Brāhmaṇa,
the worlds of the Vasus are said to be easily attained.
He who gives a young female slave endowed with beauty sports in the Nandana grove, joined by celestial nymphs.
O twice-born ones, he who goes to Umbā and Gaibhambā reaches Alakā,
where he rejoices together with Indra.
The gift of a horse is declared to be the supreme among all gifts;
likewise, the gift of a mare is remembered as yielding abundant fruit. Those who bestow horses go to the world of the Sun.
For as many hairs as there are on that horse,
for so many hundreds of years shall the fruit be tenfold for one who gives a white horse.
Just as a white cow is most excellent, so too is a white horse;
one should present a well-adorned, noble steed.
It is declared to have the *puṇḍarīka* fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
It is equipped with four oars and provided with all necessary implements.
By giving a chariot to a twice-born person, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 4] By properly giving a female elephant, one obtains this very same fruit;
by the gift of a male elephant, a man, upon descending from heaven, [attains such merit].
O twice-born ones, by giving a well-trained elephant to a Brahmin, one indeed becomes a king in this world, endowed with fame and valor.
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices by giving a chariot yoked with four elephants to a twice-born man;
one undoubtedly attains the fruit of a gift of the entire earth.
Likewise: "A man who, having purchased a tawny cow according to the prescribed rule, gives it away,
attains the fulfillment of all desires and enjoys the fruit of sacrifice."
One attains the world of cows and uplifts one's own lineage;
furthermore, by giving a buffalo, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
By giving that goat adorned [with ornaments], one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow;
by giving an unblemished goat, one is glorified in the world of Agni.
By giving a goat according to the prescribed rites, a man attains that very world;
by the gift of a buffalo, he is glorified in the world of Yama.
O best of kings, by giving a jewel one attains the world of Varuṇa;
likewise, by the gift of sight, one enjoys that very same fruit.
By the gift of wild animals, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu;
this very same fruit is declared for the gift of birds as well.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to oneself—all that should be given to the ancestors by one who desires their inexhaustible [merit]."
By this mantra, one obtains a divine celestial mansion made of gold, resembling the sun,
and filled with divine apsarases.
Vāna-khaṇḍa 4, Chapter [number]:
Hemādri.
If one gives a new, unwashed garment during the performance of a śrāddha rite,
one obtains long life, renown, sovereignty, and auspicious beauty.
Whoever gives a sacred thread and sandals during a śrāddha ceremony obtains a beautiful vehicle and comfort for his feet.
By giving a well-made fan or a palm-leaf whisk to a Brahmin,
one shall obtain a comfortable bed provided with a couch.
By always giving sandals upon the ground to Brahmins during funeral rites (śrāddha),
he obtains divine vision as well as a chariot yoked with horses.
Having become an excellent, stainless parasol adorned with garlands of flowers and the most sublime palace,
it follows after him as he goes.
By giving a shelter filled with jewels, along with beds, seats, and vessels,
to the ancestors during a śrāddha ceremony, one is honored in the heights of heaven.
He who gives pearls, lapis lazuli, garments, and various kinds of jewels,
as well as vessels completely filled with salts at a Śrāddha ceremony,
shall be attended by the essential fluids (rasas), as well as long life and good fortune.
By giving a beautiful vessel made of metal during a śrāddha rite,
one becomes a vessel for all desires, as well as for knowledge and wealth.
In the ritual of a śrāddha, one should give silver and gold;
the donor obtains abundance, as well as the power of irresistible will and wealth.
He who gives a cow at śrāddha ceremonies— one that yields a jarful of milk from a single udder—
the cows attend upon him, and likewise there is prosperity for his cattle.
Having honored the fragrant, variegated, and sweet-smelling bathing substances,
one should respectfully cause them to be given into the vessels at the time of the Śrāddha.
Demādri; Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 4.
Great rivers carrying the fetus, various pleasures,
and those who are devoted to their husbands approach the giver and purify him.
Beds, seats, vehicles, grounds, and carriages attend upon the giver; likewise, he is glorified in heaven. He who gives these things at śrāddha ceremonies obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One should respectfully cause vessels filled with sesame seeds to be given at a Śrāddha;
one obtains the merit of a thousand cows yielding jars of milk.
By giving beautiful dwellings, one becomes a partaker of the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Likewise, by giving a bed complete with ornaments, provided with pillows, well-adorned, and of various kinds, a twice-born man becomes a partaker of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
By constantly giving various male and female slaves, as well as camels, goats, and sheep, and by offering elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles at the Śrāddha rite,
and by giving various kinds of sesame seeds, one obtains imperishable fruit.
One who is engaged in the work of basket-making, being virtuous and performing auspicious deeds,
attains a beautiful state after giving away a vessel endowed with thick flowers and fruits.
Having given wells, groves, tanks, fields, wives, and houses,
one rejoices in heaven eternally as long as the moon and stars endure.
By giving a well-spread bed adorned with jewels,
his ancestors are satisfied, and he attains infinity in heaven.
Likewise, there is cloth made of silk, fine cotton, and woolen blankets;
and the purifying deer-skin from the Ruru deer, produced from the hair of wild animals.
Having given these to Brahmins and having fed them according to the prescribed rule,
the person of faith obtains the fruit that belongs to the horse sacrifice.
*Hemādri*, Chapter 4 of the *Dānakhaṇḍa*:
Silk, linen, *mārga* cloth, *dukūla*, and likewise new (*ahata*) cloth.
He who would give these [gifts] obtains unsurpassed desires.
He who gives cooked foods, parched grain with curds, sweetmeats, ghee and sugar, rice mixed with sesame, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), milk, milk-rice,
and food that is oily and warm, shall obtain the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
In the Mahābhārata: "Those men who give clothing and ornaments, as well as food, drink, and grain, and those who provide shelter for their families, go to heaven."
Those men who provide for a thousand, likewise those who give to a thousand,
and those who protect thousands, go to heaven.
O bull among the Bharatas, those men who are givers of gold and cows,
and who are bestowers of vehicles, go to heaven.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those men who provide wedding swings, spectacles,
and garments are destined for heaven.
Those men who provide monasteries, dwellings, gardens, wells, and intoxicating delights, as well as those who establish water-stations, go to heaven.
Those men by whose effort others are led away from falling into hell, or from affliction, jaundice, and other such assaults, go to heaven.
O Bhārata, those men who, having taken what was earned through service and austerities,
are free from attachment to receiving gifts, go to heaven.
Those men who have desisted from all violence, who are patient with everything,
and who have become a refuge for all, go to heaven.
O Bhārata, those men who are wealthy, powerful, and in the prime of youth,
yet remain firm-minded and have conquered their senses, go to heaven.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 4].

In the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa: "Twenty-one [gods] have been established in heaven upon the summit of Meru—those who practice non-violence and give gifts, as well as those who perform sacrifices and ascetic penances."
In these places dwelt people who were free from anger.
The twenty-one heavens—Ānanda and the others that will be mentioned immediately hereafter—are as follows:
entering water leads to Ānanda; entering fire or performing a heroic act leads to Pramoda; leaping from a cliff leads to Saumanasya; and fighting in battle leads to Atinirmala.
One who dies through fasting or through renunciation goes to the triple heaven;
one who performs the seasonal sacrifices goes to the vault of heaven, and one who maintains the sacred fires attains liberation.
O twice-born one, the performer of the *kratu* sacrifice, the performer of the *soma* sacrifice,
and the maker of tanks and wells obtain nourishment.
The giver of gold obtains good fortune, O you of great asceticism.
The man who kindles a great fire during the cold season for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings shall attain heaven and the company of apsarases.
Through the gift of gold, cattle, and land, one attains freedom from egoism;
through the pure gift of land, however, one obtains the state of peace.
By the gift of a cow, a man attains the stainless heaven;
by the gift of a horse, an auspicious day; and by the gift of a maiden, prosperity.
Having offered libations to the twice-born and having given garments with devotion,
one attains the white heaven, where having gone, one does not grieve.

A thousand, or half of that, or one hundred and eight;

I shall now fully proclaim that which, having been recited by the best of sages, brings about the attainment of the state of Gāṇapatya and destroys all sins.

The first, however, is said to be with ghee; it increases splendor by a *tulā*. With honey one gains good fortune, and with oil, abundant offspring.

For one who bows with devotion, there shall always be a cooling of the heart;

"O Tula, you are proclaimed as the standard of measure for all beings;

Having dismissed him after paying homage and feeding him according to the prescribed rules,

In that case, one should cause the mantras or the fire-oblations to be offered in this very same manner.

One should administer tin in cases of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), silver in cases of *pradara* (menorrhagia) and urinary disorders (*meha*),
and gold in all diseases, along with the fruit and rice of the *mṛtphala* plant.
Likewise, one should administer *phalodbhava* during a long-lasting and severe eclipse;
*gauḍa* in cases of *bhasmaka* disease, and the *yoga* [of *yavāgū*] in *gaṇḍamālā*.
I consider *jāṅgala* [resin] to be for the pacification of fires, while *pauṣpaka* is for the eruption of hair;

one should follow him as he departs for eight steps, O lord of men. He who bestows the Kāmadhenu according to this rite—
He goes to the heavenly world, possessing all desired objects.
O King, by giving away the entire earth when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, one obtains that same fruit through the wish-fulfilling cow; of this there is no doubt.
O King, the wish-fulfilling gem, the cow of plenty, and likewise the auspicious sixfold [set]—
the best of sages declare these three gifts to yield equal fruits.
O Lord of the Earth, such a person liberates seven generations below, seven generations above, and himself as well,
from the sins committed throughout a hundred lifetimes.
At every step, a human being obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5] | This is proclaimed as the most excellent among all gifts.
O King, this auspicious rite, which grants all desires, destroys sin,
and bestows everything, has been declared by Brahmā as the recommended expiation for all sins, even those that have arisen on a grand scale.

O King, this Kāmadhenu must be diligently performed with effort by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Śūdras for the sake of obtaining the fruits of all desires. Through the oblation of bull-dung, ghee, and sesame seeds, one should zealously offer this Kāmadhenu to the virtuous.
Having fulfilled his resolve here, he shall become the giver of the entire earth.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Kāmadhenu as described in the Vahnipurāṇa.
Now, in the Liṅgapurāṇa,
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, therefore, I shall duly explain in sequence the ritual for the golden cow,
which pacifies all sins and destroys regional famine.
It brings about the destruction of calamities and the warding off of all diseases;
one should have it fashioned with a thousand niṣkas of gold.
Or even with half of that, or again with half of that,
or with a hundred, one who is firm in his vows should properly perform it in all rites.
"In all matters" means that in cases where the amount is not explicitly stated or mentioned— such as in the delivery of gold—
one should understand that the measure ranges from a thousand down to a hundred; and this statement is incidental.
It was stated after Sulemāna: "One should fashion a cow from gold weighing from three palas up to a thousand. This is found in another manuscript as *paddhati*.
Chapter 5: On Giving,
from the Caturvargacintāmaṇi of Hemādri.
O Mahāsena, whoever gives a wish-fulfilling cow made of five hundred *palas* of gold to Śiva when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu,
by him everything up to the ends of the worlds has been given.
Thus is the doctrine of the *Kālottara*.
One should place a divine cow-form, complete with hooves and endowed with all auspicious marks;
one should set a *hiraṇya* jewel upon the tips of the hooves and a ruby (*padmarāga*) upon the horns.
O best of sages, one should place a divine pearl between the eyebrows;
one should fashion the breasts with lapis lazuli and the penis from sapphire.
It should be fashioned at the place of the teeth and adorned with all kinds of jewels;
having made it like a beast, one should fashion the calf very beautifully.
It should be made with a tenth part [of the materials] and adorned with all kinds of gems;
it is said that for the *Kāmika* [tantra], the *Vatsaka* [should be made] with a fourth part. One should then prepare a mandala in the center of the aforementioned altar.
Having placed the Surabhi cow, who possesses all kinds of jewels, in the middle of that [area],
one should wrap that Surabhi with a pair of garments.
One should worship Surabhi, the mother of all [cows], again with the Gāyatrī;
then, according to the rules, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in accordance with the prescribed ritual for the Abekāgni.
Or, having divided this [oblation] as before, one should perform the remaining rites;
the worship of Śiva should be performed by offering ghee and other substances to the Liṅga.
O Great-minded One, the deceitful man should cause that cow to be given to the Brahmins,
and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of thirty [gold pieces] should be bestowed.
The meaning is: "by means of this hymn-mantra of Gosāvitrī. The wise one should recite the mantra known as Gosāvitrī, [which is] the Gāyatrī.

Chapter 5] Thus it is stated in the Vātula.

O Kāmiketu, one should worship the Lord with ghee and other offerings, as well as with a thousand jars and so forth; having propitiated a cow with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should cause her to be given to the Brahmins.
One should first honor the preceptor with armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments;
having offered a pair of garments and made the formal request according to the prescribed rite,
a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of thirty-three gold pieces should be given, O one of great austerity.

The gift of thirty-three-fold sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), however, pertains to the subject of the single-fire rite (*ekāgni*); in the case of multiple fires, the fee is like that of the *tulāpuruṣa*.
This has been stated in the Śaiva [scriptures].

Alternatively, according to the ritual for the single fire (ekāgni), provided it is accompanied by fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial food, a gift of at least twenty niṣkas should be given to the teacher; such is the procedure for the single fire.
The option of using a single fire pertains to those with very limited wealth.
As before, regarding the question "for whom?", the meaning is that one should perform all the remaining unmentioned details exactly as prescribed for the Tulāpuruṣa rite in the Liṅga Purāṇa.
In the Kālottara [Tantra]: "He who bestows this [initiation] has given the entire world of moving and non-moving beings;
together with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall travel in celestial chariots of divine splendor."
One attains the world of Śiva for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras;
at the end of that time, one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) and, possessing wisdom, shall go to Śiva.
Thus concludes the gift of the *Kāmadhenu* according to various scriptures.
Now, the seventh great gift (*mahādāna*), known as the *Hiraṇyāśva* (Golden Horse), is described.
Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme rite of the Golden Horse (Hiraṇyāśva).
[Dānakhaṇḍa 5, Chapter 5].
Hemādri:
By whose grace one obtains the fruit of the forest [penance] which yields infinite results.
Then, having reached an auspicious lunar day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
one should perform the invocation of the worlds (lokegāvāhana) as in the rite of the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa.

A wise man, when performing the Demavājima sacrifice for those with limited means, should carry out the duties regarding the officiating priests, the sacrificial pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth, using a single fire as in the case of minor rites.

Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is included that which is prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa* for the Tulāpuruṣa gift— namely, the place, time, the ancestral rite of increase (*vṛddhiśrāddha*), the worship of Śiva and others, the selection of the preceptor and officiating priests, the offering of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the drawing of the circle upon the altar, and the consecration of the canopy, arches, and banners; [all these] being performed even in small-scale [versions].

Regarding the phrase "like fire," it has been explained that one should place [the horse] in the middle of the sacrificial ground upon black antelope skin and sesame seeds; this should be understood as being upon sesame seeds measuring one *droṇa* placed on a black antelope skin.
One should cause the horse to be wrapped in silken cloth.
According to one's capacity, the wise person [should give] more than three palas up to a thousand palas.

One should give a bed equipped with its furnishings, together with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, vessels, eight full jars, and provided with garlands and fruits, along with [an image of] the Sun.

There were various bed-appurtenances, such as coverlets, pillows, and cloths; fruits, flowers, saffron, camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, betel, mirrors, combs, chowries, fans, and seats— these vessels stood before him.
A seal-ring, a pair of sandals, a copper vessel, a water-pot, a lamp, a canopy, and so forth; "joined with Mārttaṇḍa" means one should fashion the solar disk (sūryamaṇḍala) mounted upon gold.
"Putrikā" [is so called] by those who possess many beloveds.
The Mountain of Merit (*Pemādri*). [Chapter 5 of the Section on Giving (*Dānakhaṇḍa*]:
The characteristics of the Sun were described in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.
Then, having been bathed with all medicinal herbs by the foremost of Veda-knowers,
he should recite this mantra while holding a handful of flowers.

Here too, having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the preceding day, on the second day the Guru should complete the ritual— from the recitation of the *puṇyāha* formula up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*)— as previously described. Then, the patron (*yajamāna*), bathed with water containing all medicinal herbs and wearing white garments, circumambulates [the site] three times.
Having performed the rite, one should utter the mantra to be spoken hereafter:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all gods, you who were eager to retrieve the Vedas;
in the form of a horse, protect me from this ocean of saṃsāra."
Since you yourself, having become sevenfold in the form of the meters, cause the sun to illuminate the worlds,
therefore protect us, O Eternal One.
Having thus uttered this, he should present that horse to the Guru;
by giving it, through the sun that destroys sins, he attains the eternal world.
One should honor all the officiating priests with gifts of cattle,
and one should present all kinds of grain and ritual implements to the preceptor.
Having first performed all the preliminary rites, he should indeed eat food that is free from oil;
likewise, he should cause the hearing of the Purāṇas to be performed there for the sake of his own nourishment.
The statement regarding the gift should be understood here as before:
"one should give a dakṣiṇā," such as gold according to one's capacity; for those with means, it is according to their own wealth.
"One should honor all the members and the officiating priests with cows and all kinds of grain and implements";

from this application [of the ritual act], it is understood that the placing of the grain occurs prior to the distribution. Regarding the instruction "one should present it to the Guru," in the case of giving a small amount of wealth, one should give a horse to the Ācārya himself, or according to one's capacity, [other items] excluding bones.
One should give gold and other such items; however, in the case of giving substances weighing a thousand *palas* or more, there is a specific restriction on the state [of the recipient].
[Page 308–308] Hemādri, Chapter 5 of the Section on Giving (*Dānakhaṇḍa*).

Even in the case of very few [participants], according to the view of Ekāgni, this should be observed; and therefore, as before, one should perform the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
He who performs this ritual of the golden horse,
being honored in heaven as the lord of the gods,
is freed from sin and enters the city of Murāri.
He attains [this] while being honored with water libations.
The king who recites this gift of a horse is liberated from all impurities; by means of the horse sacrifice,
he proceeds to the world of the Sun in a golden celestial chariot.
He who then beholds that which is worshipped by the wives of the Lord of the Thirty-three;
Or whatever man of little wealth hears of this gift of golden horses and remembers it with joy in this world,
he too goes forth with his sins destroyed and his body like that of a sage.
A place frequented by the gods Purandara and Maheśvara.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of a golden horse as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said: I shall now describe the gift of a golden horse, which brings about victory.
The secret doctrine is superior to ten thousand horse sacrifices.
Having performed [the rite] one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times,
one who is endowed with auspicious characteristics and joined by all the powers of withdrawal [attains success].
The term "hundred thousand" (śatasahasra) is intended as an illustration;
it refers to [mantras] beginning with the Thousand-Petalled [Lotus] and ending with the Mantrita-pila.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5] "But in the case of a small [offering], the wise man should perform the Hema-vājimakhayajña according to the rite of the single fire (ekāgni)."
Thus it is stated in the Vātula-tantra:
"One should properly have the five auspicious marks (pañcakalyāṇaka) made of silver;
because they are on the four feet, the face, and the belly, it is called the 'five auspicious marks'."
Endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of all limbs,
equipped with every weapon, the imperishable vehicle of Indra.
Having established that horse, endowed with excellent qualities and equal to Uccaiḥśravas, in the Middle Country, one should bring it back and worship it.

Having established it in the Middle Country— meaning, having placed that horse upon sesame seeds in the center of the altar-maṇḍala prescribed for the Tulāpuruṣa gift described in the Liṅga Purāṇa, which serves as the archetype for this gift—
one should worship it while meditating upon Uccaiḥśravas.

In the eastern direction of that [place], having honored a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas with the thought that he is the Lord of the Gods (Surendra), one should cause five niṣkas to be given to him.
One should give a dark-colored horse to the Brāhmaṇas according to the prescribed rule;
one should give a golden horse and likewise honor the Ācārya.
According to the extent of one's wealth, or even with five niṣkas, one should satisfy the poor,
the blind, the miserable, the protectorless, children, the elderly, the sick,
and the distressed with gifts of food, and especially the Brāhmaṇas.
One should cause the Lord—the Liṅga or the embodied Maheśvara—to sleep with ghee;
the quantity for that is exactly one hundred palas, and it is the same when using milk.
Having established [the deity] with the *brahmakūrca* mixture and having smeared it with agallochum and sandalwood,
one should worship and prostrate before the God of gods and then ask for forgiveness.
The man who, having partaken [of this], performs this gift on the new moon day—
[End of Chapter 5, Section on Gifts].
Hemādri states: Having enjoyed the worlds of Indra for a long time, one shall become a lord of kings upon this earth.

Having propitiated the Brahmins with Indrabudhas and given five *niṣkas* to those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and others, and having given gold for the horse-sacrifice (*hiraṇyākha*), he should give five *niṣkas* to his teacher (*ācārya*).
The ritual of bathing Śiva and all other preceding and subsequent procedures (*pūrvottaratantra*) are to be performed as before.
In the Matsya Purāṇa and other texts, however, the gift of the conch is said to be for the preceptor alone. But the Kāmika states:
"Having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, one should present it to the Brahmins."
Having honored Surendrabuddhi and presented him with five niṣkas,
one should perform the worship of the mandala, the fire sacrifice (homa), the installation of the ritual jar (kalaśa),
and likewise the offering of fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others, just as in the case of the Tulābhāra rite.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a golden horse as stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa.
Now begins the eighth great gift (mahādāna), named the Golden Horse Chariot, according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the most excellent great gift (mahādāna),
known as the Meritorious Horse-Chariot (aśvaratha), which destroys even the greatest sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
one should perform the invocation of the World-Guardians (Lokeśas) as in the rite of the Tulāpuruṣa gift;
[and likewise provide for] the sacrificial priests, the pavilion, the materials, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
"Like the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa": it should be understood as being like the Tulāpuruṣa mentioned in the Matsya Purāṇa;
the word "and so forth" (ādi) is also to be explained as before: having placed sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, one should have a golden chariot fashioned.
It has eight wheels, four horses, four axles, and a single pole.

It is joined with a sapphire pitcher in the form of a banner,
accompanied by the eight world-protectors, and endowed with petals of ruby.

In this context, regarding the expectation of the quantity of the sesame seeds and the chariot, there is no restrictive rule established by the person [the author], as no specific measure has been heard in the original source. However, some say that because of the proximity [of the passage], the measure of one *droṇa* for the sesame seeds—which is established in the context of gifts such as the golden *saṃhasta* chariot—is what is intended here. "The master... [end of fragment].
The axle-tree is the wood that supports the yoke;
the banner-pole is without a staff, and since the chariot is made of gold, it too must be made of gold, and it should be equipped with a pinnacle at the top made of sapphire.
The characteristics of the world-protectors (lokapālas) are stated in the Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa:
"There should be four full water-jars and ten kinds of grains."
It was covered with silken cloth and provided with a canopy above.

In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, joined with the Kṣupa constellation and accompanied by a man, whatever person is devoted to a particular deity should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) using the "Hymn of a Hundred Names" (Śatanāman).
Here, there should be a five-colored canopy; the person [representing] the chosen deity should be placed upon a golden chariot.
One should give garments, sandals, and wooden shoes;
and according to one's means, one should also give beds and seats along with cows.
A wise person, if capable, should have [the image] made from more than three palas of gold.
"The weight is two thousand *palas*; and this measurement of gold is to be understood as including the flag-bearer, the man, the world-protector (*lokapāla*), the horse, and the wheel-guardian.
It is joined with eight chariots and four chariot-horses."
From two [units] comes ten thousand (ayuta); from two [more], it is accompanied by the lion-bannered one (masiṃhadhvaja).

In the view of the eight-horse [chariot], it is joined with a golden lion; and in the view of the four-horse [chariot], a sapphire (indranīla) jar should be placed on the banner. In the view of the two-horse [chariot], there is a golden lion; such is the established rule.
(*"On the jar," according to another manuscript.)
