Hemādri.
Then both Cakrara and Cakra, these two mounted on horses,
having reached an auspicious time, were bathed by the twice-born as before.
Wearing white garlands and garments, one should offer [this] and utter this mantra:

The two wheel-protectors (cakrarakṣau), mounted on horses near the wheels, should be made as the two Aśvinī-kumāras. Gobhila states their characteristics: "The two divine physicians should be made with two arms, having horses as their vehicles."
O twice-born one, medicinal herbs should be placed in their two right hands,
and likewise, beautiful books should be placed in their two left hands.
"The auspicious time. A favorable *lagna*, *muhūrta*, and so forth for the patron (*yajamāna*).

Here too, as before, on the day following the day of consecration (*adhivāsana*), upon the completion of all rites such as the recitation of the *puṇyāha* [formula], having bathed with all medicinal herbs and water and having taken handfuls of flowers, the patron—"
Having performed three circumambulations with reverence, one should recite the following mantra:
"Homage, homage to the Destroyer of Sins."
O Soul of the Universe, whose vehicle is the Veda-steed, Lord of all abodes, source of both existence and non-existence— O forest fire to the weeds of sin, grant me peace!
You alone are the creator and the supreme treasure-house of the Vasus, Aṣṭakas, Ādityas, and Maruts;
therefore, may my heart go forth unto You.
The state of being devoid of *dharmas* arises from the destruction of sound.

Here too, the preliminary procedures— the preparation for the gift, the offering of gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the distribution of materials among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the preceptor (*ācārya*), the ownership of the substances, the ritual of the single fire (*ekāgni*), and so forth— should be understood as before; thereafter, one should perform the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, the dismissal (*visarjana*), and other such rites.
282 Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5] Now, from the Atharvaveda-mañjarī-brāhmaṇa.
Oṃ. Now, therefore, we shall set forth the procedure for the Akharatha rite.

For the removal of all sins, during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight of a month, under the Puṣya asterism, when the moon is conjoined with a favorable planet, or at the time of an eclipse; then, from the time of the offering by the officiating priest—
Then, having mounted a golden chariot and having sprinkled everything with water mixed with milk, having caused the anointing of the horses as prescribed,
having bound on garments, perfumes, and garlands, and having established the fire and taken hold of it,
he should then offer oblations with the two verses beginning "Arise, O Vājin," and [offer] the *sūrya-caru*.
Having gratified the *viṣāsahi* (the overcomer) with the mantra "sahamānam," and having touched the horse while reciting the hymn beginning with "abhimanyu," one should then offer oblations.

Having sprinkled everything—the chariot, the yoke, and the pole—with water, or having sprinkled the horse itself, one should sacrifice the *sampāta* remnants of the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) upon the heads of the three horses, reciting the mantra: "udayate namaḥ."
Having paid homage with these nine mantras, one who understands should offer libations. Regarding this,
there are two verses:
Whatever fruit has been proclaimed for all gifts whatsoever,
that one obtains by giving a horse-chariot to Brahmins according to the prescribed rite.
Having attained the stainless state, which is unassailable even by the gods, well-earned, golden,
and adorned with gold, he is liberated from sin.
He sports with the Lord of Chariots in the divine world of the Sun.
In the Mayapurāṇa:
"Thus, he who performs this gift of a horse-chariot, which destroys the fear of speed..."
Having cast off the veil of all impurities,
one attains the supreme state of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
[Page 314] The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 5: Hemādri.
[He who has] surpassed the power [of others] with his brilliantly shining body...
O Indra, having entered the mandala of the fierce-rayed sun,
may you long enjoy the splendor of the lotus of his face, being drunk in by the bee-like eyes of the Siddha women.
Whoever thus recites or hears this account of the gift of a chariot drawn by golden horses shall never go to the city of hell.
He goes once again to the abode of Varakaripu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the chariot with golden wheels.
Now begins the ninth great gift (mahādāna), known as the Golden Elephant Chariot.
In the Matsya Purāṇa, Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the auspicious golden elephant-chariot,
by the gift of which a human being indeed attains the realm of Viṣṇu.
Then, having reached an auspicious lunar day, the wise man should perform the recitation by Brahmins and the invocation of the world-protectors, as in the ritual of the Tulāpuruṣa gift.
The officiating priests, the sacrificial pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings,
and so forth— here too, one should fast and partake of a meal together with the Brahmins.

In this context, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), all that has been omitted— such as the place, time, fire-sacrifice, and so forth— is to be understood as it is established in the *Matsya Purāṇa* regarding the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite. Regarding the term "having fasted" (*upoṣita*),
it should be understood that even a single night's fast applies for those who are unable to observe a full fast.
One should construct it in the shape of a lotus, made of gold and adorned with jewels,
provided with various balconies and equipped with four towers.
[The mandala] consisting of the eight world-protectors (lokapālas), together with Śiva, the Sun, and Brahmā.
Hemādri:
[Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5] In the center, it should be accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, together with Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi.

The flower-chariot (*puṣparatha*), a chariot for the purpose of play, is covered above in the shape of a quadrangular courtyard; from its enclosures (*valaya*) emerge the supports of the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*), characterized by Brahmā, Śiva, and the Sun, who are liberated.

In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*, the word "middle" (*madhya*) is connected with both "eastern" and "western," because even for Śiva and the others, their respective positions are established by that very [term].
The characteristics of Nārāyaṇa and so forth are derived from the *Pañcarātra*.
Nārāyaṇa has four arms; in his upper left hand he holds a conch, and likewise a discus;
in his right hand he holds a great lotus that resembles a mass of clouds.
In the left [hand], there is a fist with the hand of Śrīkī, and the other has a lotus in its hand.
Having placed a drona-measure of sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, one should establish the chariot;
likewise, the eighteen types of grains, along with vessels, seats, and sandalwood.
One should provide a lamp, shoes, sandals, and a mirror;
on the flagstaff, one should place Garuḍa, and at the tip of the pole, Vināyaka.
It is endowed with the fruit of the Name,
and above it is a canopy made of five-colored silk, adorned with jasmine flowers.
It was accompanied by four water-jars and eight cows,
and by four horses adorned with pearl necklaces.
Having fashioned [the image] according to its true form and joined it with two elephants, one should present it;
one should make it from five palas up to a bhāra, according to one's capacity.
"One should fashion Garuḍa upon the banner," and so forth; "banner" (dhvaja) refers to the staff.
The characteristics of Garuḍa are described in the Nāradīya:
"In front of Indra, the bird [Garuḍa], whose hair is like Guḍākeśa (Arjuna), stands with palms joined in reverence."
Reaching the middle of the knees upon the ground, it is adorned with a serpent’s hood at its tip.
Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5: Cemādri.
[He should have] the shanks of a bird, the neck of a man, a prominent nose, and the limbs of a man.
The son of Vinatā should be made with short arms and joined wings.
Now, regarding Vināyaka:
here, he should be depicted as having four arms and three eyes, with the face of an elephant,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, and having the moon as his crest-ornament.
One should place a tusk in the right hand, a rosary in the second,
an axe in the third, and likewise a sweetmeat in the fourth.

"Teeth and so forth are to be given in the upper and lower hands"—thus the *kūvara* has been explained. "Unfading flower" refers to a specific type of blossom; this follows the maxim that a conventional term conveys its meaning through its etymological derivation.
The term *mahāsaha* is understood as it is well-known; the "burden" (*bhāra*) has been explained.
And the deities residing on the banner [are to be made] of gold, measured at five *palas* and so forth, like those on a chariot.

These [materials] are not to be produced; rather, having prepared the requisites as before and performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), and having completed the entire ritual procedure (*karmakāṇḍa*) such as the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) over the days,
the preceptor (*ācārya*) shall perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) of the patron (*yajamāna*) with waters containing all medicinal herbs.
Then, amidst auspicious sounds,
the barber, having circumambulated [the child] three times to the right while holding a handful of flowers in his hands,
should recite this mantra and announce it to the Brāhmaṇas.

Homage, homage to you, O God! You are worshipped by Śaṅkara, Padmaja, Arka, Lokeśa, Vidyādhara, and Vāsudeva. O Ancient One, composed of the splendor of sacrifice, protect me from that which causes trembling.
O Lord, that most secret state of Murāri, which is the cause of bliss and whose nature consists of qualities within,
which sages behold in yoga and in meditative absorption— [that] you are; you have ascended the chariot.
Cemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5] [[page 317-to-317]]
Since you alone are the vessel for the drinking of the sacrificial nectar that holds the treasure of bliss for those dwelling in the ocean of worldly existence, therefore,
show favor by making this proclamation.
They were well-suited for chariots made of refined gold because of their excellent craftsmanship.

Having prostrated with the chanting of mantras according to one's ability and having prepared a gift of gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should recite the ritual formula (*prayoga*) as before and bestow that elephant-chariot, together with a living elephant, upon the Brahmins;
the distribution of the four parts and so forth among the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others, as well as giving to others with his permission, should follow.

"That [act] fulfills the needs of the poor and the helpless; therefore, one should proceed according to the standard ritual procedure. Then, when the *puṇyāha-vācana* has been performed, the patron (*yajamāna*) should go near the altar (*vedi*) and perform the worship of the deities. However, the Āsuri school may omit this; for it is stated in the *Gopatha-brāhmaṇa* of the Atharvaveda: 'Now, therefore, [concerning] the gift of elephants and chariots...'"
I shall describe the ritual procedure:
having fashioned a chariot made of gold with beautiful wheels,
one should worship it according to the rules with seven elephants.
Alternatively, it may be made of gold or silver, joined with four [parts],
or even made of wood, untouched [by flaws] and filled with all necessary materials.
One who has it encircled by a pair of elephants or a pair of bulls enjoys the earth with its seven continents for seven births.

On the full moon or new moon day when the moon is in conjunction with the *Hasta* asterism, or on another auspicious lunar day—having established this fire facing east according to the ritual procedure prescribed for that region—and having taken hold of it, he should then offer oblations:
"To Savitṛ, svāhā! To Patana, svāhā! To Pāva..."

"Kāyasvāhā, sahasraraśmaye svāhā, mārtaṇḍāya svāhā, viṣṇave svāhā, prajāpataye svāhā, parameṣṭhine svāhā"— having thus [recited], "hastiṣaṃsasprathata-saṃyuktam" is another reading in the *Pulaka* manuscript.
The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 5:
Hemādri.

287. Having brought the remnants of the libations into the large jar (*vṛhatkalasa*), and having sprinkled everything with the formula, "The yoke, the yoke-halter, the chariot," he should yoke it with the formula, "With the mind of the sacrifice, I yoke thee."
I yoke you, the weary one, with my mind, and the foremost one for the highest draught.
Be a leader for those who run; let him who is yoked give half [the prize] to the one who is joined.
He whose chariot rolls on with auspicious birds, O Agni, the peaceful finder of wealth—[he is] the one who possesses the golden, silver-hued [chariot].
May Savitṛ, with golden hands, protect us. May he,
who strikes with his hand from within the many chariots yoked together,
cause one to attain the auspicious, divine station of Savitṛ, which possesses the speed of desire.

In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "He who, having thus prostrated, causes the gift of a golden chariot to be made, shall have his body liberated from all sins and be honored by hosts of Vidyādharas, gods, and lords of sages."
He attains that state beyond the senses of the Moon-crested Lord.
Even those kinsmen who partake in the distress of the burning caused by contact with the smoke arising from the spreading mass of their committed evils.
And one who has given gifts of elephants and chariots leads all his fathers and grandsons, without exception, even from Raurava to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of golden elephants and chariots.
Now, the tenth great gift, known as the Pañcalāṅgala, is set forth. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift known as Pañcalāṅgalaka, which destroys even the most heinous sins.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day, such as the beginning of a Yuga or an eclipse,
a man should bestow a gift of land endowed with five furrows.
Hemādri: [The Section on Giving, Chapter 5]
He may give a Karyaṭa, a Kheṭaka, or a village rich in crops;
or a hundred Nivartanas, or even half of that, according to his capacity.
The skillful one, having fashioned five plows out of heartwood,
equipped them with all necessary implements, and likewise made five others of gold.
The nature of a *karvaṭa* and other such places is described in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "A city has high ramparts and walls, is surrounded on all sides by moats,
measures one and a half *yojanas* in width, and is eight parts in length."
Half of that [distance] is a *kheṭa*, and half of that again is a *karvaṭa*;
likewise, there are places consisting mostly of artisans and very prosperous farmers.

"He dwells in the midst of a field, a portion of land known as a village. As for the measurement of the area being returned, it will be stated later that it is by means of a staff seven cubits long, and so forth.
"Sāradāru" refers to heartwood such as *māka*, *iṅgudī*, sandalwood, and so forth; "implements" refers to the yoke, thongs, linchpins, ropes, goads, and the like.
[One should acquire] ten oxen endowed with auspicious marks that are capable of bearing the burden.

One should consecrate them in the hall, adorned with golden horns and ornaments, decorated with pearl tassels, having silver hooves and forehead marks, clothed in red silk garments, and provided with garlands and sandalwood paste.
The characteristics of a bull include being well-behaved, youthfulness, virility, freedom from disease, and the ability to endure hardships,
among others. Furthermore, [the bulls] have silver hooves and silver tilakas on their foreheads.
One should cook a sacrificial pap (caru) made of milk-rice for Parjanya, Āditya, and the Rudras;
one should present this caru to him in a single cooking-pot alone.
Endowed with the fragrance of sandalwood. This reading is found in another manuscript of mine.
[Page 320–320] Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5: Hemādri.
One should offer palāśa fuel-sticks, as well as clarified butter and black sesame seeds.

Here too, having performed the preliminary rites such as the consecration (*adhivāsana*) as before, and having conducted the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) on the following day, one should complete the remainder of the ritual, beginning with the seating of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at the sacrificial fire-pits (*agnikuṇḍa*).
However, there is this further distinction here:

from among the officiating priests prescribed for the *tulāpuruṣa* homa, the preceptor (*guru*) should designate one of them; that single priest alone, at a single sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [should perform the rite] for Parjanya, Āditya, and the Rudras with their respective characteristic mantras, using materials such as milk-rice (*pāyasa-caru*) and so forth, [in the number of] one hundred and eight.
One should offer a thousand oblations.
The wise man should perform the invocation of Lokeśa as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite;
then, with auspicious sounds, the wise man [should proceed] with white garlands and garments.
The couple should adorn each other with golden threads, rings, silken garments, fine woolens, and jewels.
One should give a bed with its furnishings and a single milch cow;
likewise, one should cause eighteen kinds of grain to be placed all around it.
Then, having circumambulated [the deity] and holding a handful of flowers,
one should recite this mantra and then offer everything as an oblation.

The invocation of Lokeśa is merely an illustration; for herein [are included] the selection of the place and time, the ancestral offering (*vṛddhi-śrāddha*), the worship of Śiva and others, the recitation by Brahmins,

the selection of the preceptor (*guru*) and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the offering of honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the altar (*vedikā*), the canopy (*vitāna*), and the drawing of the wheel (*cakralekhana*).
The raising of the victory banner (*racapatākā*) and so forth is understood as that prescribed in the *Matsyapurāṇa* for the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite.

Regarding the word "then" (*tataḥ*): the grammatical connection is that after the fire-oblation (*homānantaram*), having bathed in water containing all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhijalasnātaḥ*) and wearing white garments (*śuklāmbaradharaḥ*), one should give. As for the phrase "this pair of twice-born [bride and groom]" (*dvijadampatyaṃ*), it refers to the preceptor (*guru*) who is appointed to perform the entire ritual.

Since there is no cognition of [the gift] being for the south or the other [direction], and because there is no reason to abandon what is proximate, and because the word "twice-born" (dvija) is not in conflict [with the teacher's status], it is understood that the gift should be given to the preceptor himself together with his wife.
Hemādri, Chapter 5 of the Dānakhaṇḍa (Section on Gifts), page 321.

With his permission, it should be given to others as well; even when [the property] is small, the rule for the single fire (ekāgni) must be observed. The bed and its furnishings have been explained in the section on the offering of gold.
Now, the mantra:
Since all the hosts of gods, as well as all things mobile and immobile,
stand supported by your shoulders, O Lord, may there be devotion to Śiva within me.

And because other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of land, [one should think]: "May my devotion to Dharma alone become firm. Having spoken this mantra, one should prepare a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity, following the previously mentioned procedure.
One should perform [the rites], and thereafter the recitation for an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and their dismissal (*visarjana*).
Thirty *daṇḍas*—each *daṇḍa* being seven cubits long—constitute a *nivartana*.
Prajāpati states that a *gocarma* measures three-quarters of that.
If a wise person should offer a hundred circumambulations with this mantra according to this rite,
the entire mass of his sins is swiftly destroyed.
Or he may give even half of that, or even a mere *gocarma* (cow-hide) area, or even just the space required for a dwelling; such a person is also liberated from sins.
As many furrows as there are on the surface of the earth, so many hairs as there are on the body of the daughter of Bhāṣāpati (the Earth), for that long shall he remain in the city of Śaṅkara.
The person who makes a gift of land here in this world...
Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Suras, Asuras, and Siddhas all approached him with waving whisks;
together with his father, grandfather, and kinsmen, he was honored with great majesty.
"By means of slow-moving chariots"—this is a reading found in some manuscripts.
[Page 322] *Dānakhaṇḍa*, Chapter 5: Hemādri.
And becoming a leader of the immortals, he goes to the city of Śambhu.
Even the status of Indra is attained by one who makes a gift of land, oxen, and ploughs; therefore,
the gift of land brings about results that are visible even in this very life.
Even that which is subject to destruction, when offered as a gift, leads to the arising of supreme prosperity.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the five ploughs as declared in the glorious Matsya Purāṇa.
The Blessed Lord said:
Hereafter, I shall describe to you another wonderful gift.
O Indra among kings, by giving this, one becomes a bestower of all gifts at all times.
The gift known as the "ploughed row" (saṃyuktahalapaṅkti), which pacifies all sins and bestows all desired objects, grants every fruit.
A row is said to consist of ten ploughs, and a plough consists of four yokes;
the wise say that the ten blades are made of solid wood.
Golden headbands, radiant with jewels and auspicious;
youths who were strong, handsome, free from physical defects, and well-adorned.
A man should yoke bulls with auspicious limbs to those ploughs, their heads anointed with sandalwood and other unguents, and adorned with garments, gold, and flowers.
One should have the yokes made joined in pairs and equipped with thongs,
as well as the goads, pins, fastenings, and all other necessary implements.
With such ploughs, one should construct a continuous row of fields,
whether it be a small hamlet, a mountain settlement, or a village abounding in crops.
In another manuscript, the reading is "caturgavaminī.
282 Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5]
One should calculate either a hundred nivartanas or even half of that;
with a disciplined mind, one should give such a gift during the time of a festival.

One should cause [the gift] to be given on the full moon day of Kārttika or Vaiśākha, likewise during the northern transit of the sun (uttarāyaṇa), at the time of one's birth, during an eclipse, or at the equinoxes (viṣuva).
He should invite an even number of Brahmins who are perfected in the Vedas, whose limbs are unimpaired, well-adorned, learned in the scriptures,
and humble.
A wise man should have a pavilion constructed measuring ten cubits;
on the preceding day, he should also prepare one beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit.
There, those best of the twice-born should perform the oblation with the *vyāhṛtis*;
they should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to Pajanya, Aditya, and the Rudras, according to the rule.
He should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, as well as clarified butter and black sesame seeds;
then, having seated the auspicious row of guests in the midst of the grain, he should proceed.
Then, having bathed in the presence of all [the deities], wearing white garments and being pure,
the sacrificer, with a concentrated mind, yokes the row of ploughs.
Amidst the sounds of conchs and trumpets and abundant recitations of the Veda,
one who has taken a handful of flowers should utter this mantra.
Since all the hosts of celestial beings always stand upon the plow,
supported upon the shoulders of the bull, may my devotion be fixed upon Śiva.
And because other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the gift of land, may my devotion to this always remain firm.
When this has been said, then that best of the twice-born should cause the row to proceed with the immortal seeds and likewise with *sujata*.
One should offer [the oblation] among those who are deluded by cooking for themselves.
[Page 324] *Dānakhaṇḍa*, Chapter 5: Hemādri.
The wise person should continue until three circumambulations have been completed, and then desist;
thereafter, having performed a circumambulation and having offered gifts to the Brahmins.
Having prostrated with the offering of a cow and a sacrificial fee, one should dismiss [the deity].
Whoever bestows this gift according to this rite is honored in the heavenly world, together with twenty-one generations of his lineage.
For seven births, one shall not behold poverty, misfortune, or diseases; likewise, one shall become a sovereign of the earth.
But by merely seeing the gift being given, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one is liberated from the sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt.
This gift was given in ancient times by Dilīpa,
Yayāti, Śibi, Nimi, and the wise Bharata;
by the power of this gift, they even now rejoice in heaven.
O protector of the earth, O best of kings, this gift should be given with effort by one endowed with devotion—
whether by a woman or by a man.
O King, if a row of five, four, or three [ploughs] cannot be found,
even a single plough should be given according to the prescribed rule by those who are wise.
For as many particles of dust as there are in the earth turned up by the tip of a plow,
and for as many hairs as there are on the body of a well-bred draft ox,
for that many yugas shall he dwell in the city of Śaṅkara.
The man who here provides food for the row [of guests].
One should cause this row of ploughs, yoked with extremely powerful bulls,
to be given to the most excellent of the twice-born along with abundant food on an auspicious day;
"it is equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice," so says a certain reading.
Cemādri: [Chapter on the Section on Giving] | Those virtuous ones who desire to possess the earth become worthy recipients by approaching the presence of kings.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the row of ploughs as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Now, the great gift known as the "Gift of Eleven Earths" (*ekādaśadharādāna*) is described.
In the *Śrī Matsyapurāṇa*, the Fish [incarnation] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed gift of the earth,
which effects the destruction of the sins of men and the eradication of inauspiciousness.
One should have fashioned a golden earth resembling Jambudvīpa,
complete with its boundary mountains and containing my own abode in its center.
It is endowed with the eight world-protectors, possessed of the nine continents,
filled with hundreds of rivers and streams, and surrounded on its outskirts by the ocean.

"Anukāriṇīm" means "accompanied by a companion. For here, when it is said that one should make [the city] similar to Jambudvīpa, it attains a resemblance to the earth endowed with all its mountains, cities, lakes, forests, and so forth; thus, by the words "possessing boundary-mountains" and so on, [it is shown to be] only that much—

It is understood that this is an imitation of the earth as it is currently constituted; otherwise, since that [earth] would already be understood in its general sense, there would be the consequence of the uselessness of the specific qualification. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: when it is said, "One should make this earth sevenfold," since the [entire] earth consisting of seven continents (*saptadvīpavatī*) would be implied, it is stated that it should be an imitation of Jambūdvīpa; even in that case, not [all of it].

In the context of imitating those possessed of mountains, [the phrase] "possessing boundary-mountains" is used; likewise, when there is the possibility of imitating Meru, [the phrase] "possessing Mount Meru in the center" is used; and for the purpose of excluding various hosts of gods, [the phrase] "endowed with the eight world-protectors" is used. And thus, by resorting to this number of items, the Purāṇas—
In some places, the reading is "the application of the water-pot [offering] to the possessor of the seven islands" (*saptadvīpavatyāḥ karakaprasaṅgaḥ*).
Alternatively, there is also the reading "relying on the concise method" (*saṃkṣepapakṣāśrayaḥ*).
Hemādri, Chapter 5 of the Dānakhaṇḍa, page 326.
The phrase "endowed with nine years" is stated for the purpose of including the four-year period and so forth shown in the interval, thereby ensuring the completion [of the cycle].
Regarding this, Jambūdvīpa is described in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
O Maitreya, this Jambūdvīpa, nine thousand yojanas in extent and one hundred thousand yojanas in width, has been described by me to you in brief.
O Maitreya, having encircled Jambudvīpa, the Ocean of Butter, which is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, stands outside in the form of a ring.
Jambudvīpa stands in the center of all the continents;
and in its center, O Maitreya, is the golden mountain Meru.
Its height is eighty-four thousand yojanas;
its foundation extends sixteen thousand yojanas, and it is thirty-two thousand yojanas wide at the summit.
At its base, its circumference is sixteen thousand [yojanas] on all sides.
In another Purāṇa, however, it is stated that its height is sixty-eight yojanas.

Likewise: "O highly fortunate one, there, to the four directions of Meru, lies Ilāvṛta, nine thousand yojanas in extent; and there are four mountains acting as buttresses for Meru, each ten thousand yojanas in height."
To the east is the mountain named Mandara, to the south is Gandhamādana;
Vaibhrāja is on the western side, and Supārśva is recorded to be in the north.
The boundary mountains (*maryādāparvata*) have been shown in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Furthermore, the Jāṭhara and Devakūṭa mountains are in the eastern direction."
These two extend from south to north, reaching as far as Nīla and Niṣadha.
"From the middle," according to the manuscript [re 1,
Cemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5] Kailāsa and Himavat are the two excellent mountains in the south; these two extend from the east and are situated reaching to the edge of the ocean.
Viśṛṅga and Jārudhi are the two northern excellent mountain ranges;
these two extend from east to west and are situated at the edge of the ocean.
Niṣadha and Pārijāta are the two western boundary mountains;
they extend from south to north, reaching as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains.
These are the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains.
However,
this will be stated later:
"endowed with the eight world-protectors," meaning Indra and the other seven, who constitute those eight world-protectors.

The characteristics were previously stated in the section on the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa; their placement upon Mount Meru should be performed starting from the east and proceeding in a clockwise direction through the cardinal directions.
"Endowed with nine regions"—
and the description of these regions is found in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"That which lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains..."
This indeed is called Bhārata, wherein the lineage of the Bhāratas resides.
O twice-born one, Bhārata is the first region; after that, Kiṃpuruṣa is remembered;
likewise, Harivarṣa is another to the south of Meru;
to the north is the region Ramyaka, and following that is Hiraṇmaya.
The Uttarakurus are just like Bhārata;
Bhadrāśva is to the east of Meru, and Ketumāla is to the west.
O best of the twice-born, when the [entire] region is thus described, Ilāvṛta is situated between those two; each of these [nine divisions] measures nine thousand [yojanas].
*In another manuscript, it reads "dhotaraṃ varṣam" (a rain of gold).
Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 6: Hemādri, p. 287.
Likewise: Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha are on the south;
Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin are the mountain ranges on the north.
Their height is two thousand [yojanas], and their width is the same;
two in the middle are one hundred thousand [yojanas] in measure, and the others are ten less than that.
Regarding the passage beginning with "measuring one hundred thousand," it should be understood that the two mountains, Nīla and Niṣadha, which lie on both sides of Ilāvṛta,

are each one hundred thousand *yojanas* in length. Furthermore, the two mountains Śveta and Hemakūṭa situated there should be known to measure ninety thousand *yojanas*, and likewise, the two mountains Śṛṅgin and Himavat—

The meaning is that they are eighty thousand *yojanas* in measure. The reasoning for this is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "Due to the circular nature of the island, its contraction and expansion are proclaimed.
[This is also stated] in the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*.
To the western part of Meru, measuring nine thousand [yojanas],
lies the Gandhamādana mountain, thirty-four thousand [yojanas] in extent.
Forty thousand [yojanas] from the surface of the earth is the Parigha [ocean];
when its depth is one thousand [yojanas], its width is double that.
To the east, the Mālyavat mountain is proclaimed to be of the same measurement.

In this context, since it is impossible to construct the earth and other elements with dimensions of hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* and so forth, one should instead conceive of measurements such as finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in place of thousands of *yojanas*, and practice according to the gradations of number as described. Regarding the phrase "purified by a hundred rivers and streams," the [first] river is the Bhāgīrathī.

Regarding the rivers such as the Śoṇa and others, since it is impossible to describe them in their entirety, one should provide a representation to the extent possible. At the end, the phrase "surrounded by the ocean" is used; for although the ocean is exactly the same size as the earth, it is nevertheless taught here merely as a figurative representation.
One should perform only that which is possible to imitate.
[In another manuscript, it reads "of the measure of a lac.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa,
Chapter 6] Adorned with great jewels and joined with the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas,
it should be made from a thousand *pala*s of gold, or half that amount, or according to one's capacity.
One may fashion it with three hundred, two hundred, or even one hundred [palas];
even if unable, a wise person should make it from at least five palas.
The wise man should perform the invocation of Lokeśvara like the Tulāpuruṣa rite,
including the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth.
Having spread a black antelope skin upon the altar, one should place sesame seeds upon it,
as well as the eighteen types of grain and the flavors, such as salt and the rest.
Likewise, one should arrange eight full water-pots all around,
as well as a silk canopy and various kinds of fruits.
Likewise, having fashioned beautiful pieces of cloth and fragments of sandalwood,
he performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for her.
Wearing white garments and adorned with white ornaments,
he then performed a circumambulation while holding a handful of flowers.

"Great jewels," and so forth: great jewels such as rubies (*māṇikya*) and others are shown in the technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*). The forms of Vanu, Rudra, and Arka have been mentioned in the *Brahmāṇadāna*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "clothing and so forth," [are included] place, time, the *vṛddhiśrāddha*, the worship of Śiva and others, and the recitation by Brahmins.

Everything beginning with the mental consecration (*adhivāsana*) should be performed as described in the *Tulāpuruṣa* rite; it should be noted that the jars must be full and provided with garlands, perfumes, the five gems, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, and mango shoots; the canopy should be of five colors;
and "having circumambulated" means having performed the circumambulation three times; furthermore, this includes the rites of circumambulation and so forth.

On the second day, after the completion of the remaining rites ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, and following the bathing with all medicinal herbs (*sarva-oṣadhi*), one should join [the two halves of the jar]. Then,
having attained an auspicious moment (*puṇyakāla*), one should recite these mantras.
The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 6:
Cemādri.
Salutations to you, O Vasundharā, for you are the sole abode of all the gods and the nurse of all beings; therefore, protect me.
Since you hold the Vasus and are exceedingly pure like the Vasu, the Earth (Vasundharā) was born from you; therefore, protect me thoroughly from fear.
Even the Four-faced One (Brahmā) cannot reach the end of you, O Immovable One;
therefore, salutations to you who are infinite—protect me from the mire of saṃsāra.
You alone are Lakṣmī in Govinda; as Śivā you abide as Gaurī;
you are Gāyatrī at the side of Brahmā, moonlight in the moon, and radiance in the sun.
Intellect (buddhi) is known as Brāhmī, while wisdom (medhā) resides among the sages;
because she stands pervading the universe, she is therefore considered Viśvambharā.
O Goddess, protect us from the ocean of saṃsāra with these forms: Ṭaji, Cit, Camā, Cogī, Pṛthī, Vasumatī, and Rasā.
Having thus addressed that goddess, one should present her to the Brahmins.
Or one should bestow a fourth part of the land upon the preceptor.
Then, having prostrated before the officiating priests, he should dismiss them with whatever remains.
Here too, as before, having uttered the formula of giving preceded by water, the gift is given with the permission of the preceptor;
there is also giving to others for the fulfillment of the poor and the helpless. In the case of a very small [gift], however, the procedure involves a single fire (*ekāgni*). [The land...]

Regarding the rites that must be performed, it should be understood that the gift of a village and so forth is for one capable of doing so, whereas the gift of gold according to one's means is for one who is incapable. Then, after the recitation by the Brāhmaṇas, one should perform the worship and dismissal of the deities. In the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda, it says: "Now..."

Having fasted for a kalpa under the asterism Rohiṇī, he [attains] Brahman, as if by the essence of seeds scattered upon the earth by a lord of the earth who has strewn jewels and perfumes— so it is stated in another manuscript.

The donor sprinkles [the recipient] with a jar filled with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*) while reciting the prescribed consecration mantras. He enters the vow (*vrata*) with the formula, "O Lord of Vows, by this vow... Thereafter, they both eat only what is unasked for and sleep on the ground. They observe the ritual service of the vow for one night, five nights, or twelve nights, according to their ability.
Having observed the vow, on the following day, having performed the ritual procedure up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, and having taken hold [of the sacrificer],

he should then offer oblations of clarified butter with the *Kāmasūkta*, the *Kālasūkta*, and the *Puruṣasūkta*. Then, having brought a golden representation of the earth— a model of the earth measuring one *gocarma*— and having established it upon the sacrificial altar, he should [proceed] upon this altar.

Having established those hills as "these are mountains," he should adorn the mountains with gold dust, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth; having fashioned the rivers with the *sāman* "yad ahaḥ saṃprayātāḥ" and "mandasānaḥ," he should fill them with liquids; [he recites] "aparam agram asi samudra..."
"Flow forth, release [the offering]," with these words he pours out the oceans together with the gods.

"O Bṛhaspati, lead [us] by counsel," with this he addresses the trees and others at the sacrifice. "I intend you with my mind"—thus she becomes one whose intention is fulfilled here. "Bearing the treasure," having thus caused the salutation to be made, he carries the truth.
One should have the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) proclaimed with the verse from the *Spatyanuvāka*: "The gods who are eleven in heaven," and then conclude the rite.
Having consecrated it with the mantra, "From heaven, O gods, [come] by your knowledge," one should give it to the Brahmins.
For the giver, this [gift] is a cow of Rohiṇī, which brings about either his desire or his lack of desire, or indeed suffering.
Just as seeds sprout upon the surface of the earth when tilled by the plow,
so indeed do desires sprout after death through the constant activity of the mind.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for all gifts whatsoever,
one obtains that by giving land to Brahmins according to the prescribed rite.
Now, in the Matsya Purāṇa: "He who, when a meritorious time has arrived, gives a beautiful golden earth according to this rite, goes indeed to the abode of Viṣṇu."
"maprāpamavi" is an alternative reading.
Chapter 6 of the Dānakhaṇḍa: Ciemādri.
Having gone to the city of Nārāyaṇa by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) as radiant as the sun and garlanded with networks of tinkling bells, one shall then dwell there for three kalpas.
And he shall deliver twenty-one generations, including sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
Whoever recites this in such a manner, or even hears it incidentally, shall have their body liberated from all sides by celestial palaces at the end of the eon;
they go to heaven, being entreated by the wives of the immortals.
The station of the Moon-crested Lord, served by thousands of immortals.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of land.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, Sanatkumāra said:
"I shall briefly describe the gift of gold and earth."
At the previously mentioned place and time, one should perform [the rite] together with the sages.
According to the prescribed characteristics, as before, one should cause a divine ground to be prepared either in a well or in a pavilion, even if it is only a thousand [square units] in size.
It should be made with one hand, square and very beautiful,
and endowed with the seven continents, oceans, and mountains.
It should be endowed with all sacred fords (tīrthas) and mountains, and contain Mount Meru in its center;
or else, one should fashion a nine-division island from the middle.
Having performed everything as previously described within the mandala, in the center of the altar,
one should first perform a thousand oblations according to the prescribed rule, using one-seventh part [of the materials].
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) previously prescribed should be given to the Brahmins;
and one should worship Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara, with a thousand jars and other offerings.
In this *liṅga*, it is declared that there is a mountain of golden ground;
this is the meaning according to the sages and the self-restrained brahmins.
302 Hemādri. [[page 333-to-333]]
[The Section on Giving, Chapter 6]:

It should be understood that "by a thousand" refers to a thousand *pala*s of gold; thus, as stated by Matsya, one should fashion it from five *pala*s up to a thousand *pala*s. Furthermore, it is one cubit in measure, four-sided, and seven—*pala*s?—high.
It should be made for those possessing [sufficient] wealth; "or else" (*athavā*) indicates an alternative view intended for those with very little wealth. He explains that very point:

"by one-seventh part," meaning by the seventh part of a thousand [gold pieces]. The meaning is that one should fashion it as having nine sections, the size of Jambūdvīpa. Regarding the phrase "to the Brāhmaṇas," the plural number implies many fires.
"The fivefold object is as before" means it is like the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa* mentioned in the *Liṅga Purāṇa*.
In the *Kālottara*, it says: "Listen briefly here, O Six-faced One (*Ṣaṇmukha*), to the gift of the earth.
Earth is considered to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior."
The supreme [mandala] is proclaimed to have an extent of one hundred koṭis;
that which extends to the seven continents is declared to be the middling.
One should fashion three types of maidens with Jambūdvīpa as the limit;
the best [type] should be fashioned from five bhāras of gold.
With two thousand [units], one should designate the twelve mountains; with half of that, the Tāraka-janma-karma, and likewise the Padma.
The twelve mountains, however, are to be understood as being progressively higher than Meru in the *Kālottara*.
[The lotus] made of silver (*tāraja*) is declared to be the best; that made of copper is considered middling; and the inferior one is made of iron.
Here, according to the division for the well and the lotus, there is a threefold decrease. For those who chant the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas, [the offering is] for Śiva—
One should bestow [the gift] upon devotees,
upon those who recite the four-footed and six-fold categories of meaning, and upon those who recite the Saṃhitās;
it should also be given to those who are like the tortoise and the earth-born.
Having understood the knowledge regarding the remaining [planets] according to the proper rule, one should report it;
at the eclipse of the sun, O child, one should offer a calf before Śiva.
The reading "nirvapet" appears in another manuscript.
[Page 334] Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 6.
Cemādri says: One should arrange thirteen mountains there like Meru;
one should fashion Meru there with a thousand palas.
By a multiplication of one thousand, there are twelve mountains;
each of the planets is recorded as being joined with four hundred [mountains].

In the same way, the zodiacal signs (rāśis) are to be imagined, and the constellations (nakṣatras) from half of that; likewise, the islands such as Jambūdvīpa and so forth are to be imagined like the planets.
The seven beginning with Cāra, likewise the eight divine wombs (devayoni) beginning with Aṣṭaka,
those beginning with Mṛga, and likewise Brahmā and the others, as well as the Daṅguvas.
One should cause the seven netherworlds, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūrloka,
the thousand-petaled tortoise,
and the nine-petaled lotus-born [universe] to be offered for a Kalpa before Śiva and the Śiva-brahmins.

The earth should be given to those who are firm in their vows, whose bodies are unblemished, and who are knowers of the Vedas and their established conclusions; likewise, one should bestow many forms of wealth upon them.
He whose forms are many and who is more terrible than the terrible is Bahurūpī; [this refers to] the Aghora mantra:
"From the non-terrible ones, and from the terrible ones, and from those more terrible than the terrible..."
One should offer oblations to all forms of Śarva and Rudra from every side; while the solar disc is being seized by Rāhu,
one should perform the ritual offering according to the prescribed rules and cause it to be presented before the fire with such a formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
Indeed, for as many atoms as there are in the universe,
for that many thousands of kalpas one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
His ancestors rejoice and move about as they please;
until the end of the lifespan of Rudra, they dwell in the world of Rudra.
Hemādri, Section on Gifts (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 6, Verse 304. [[page 335-to-335]]
At the end of that, they indeed become possessors of great splendor through devotion to Śiva;
pride arises in them due to their lack of insight into the true nature of Śiva.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the golden earth.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, hereafter I shall proclaim [the rite] for you.
The gift known as the "Gifting of Jambudvīpa" is the most supreme among all gifts.
By the gift of which a person indeed attains the world of Viṣṇu;
it causes the destruction of all sins and brings about all auspiciousness.
Thus, it bestows health and prosperity, increases excellent longevity for men,
grants enjoyment and liberation, and is auspicious, yielding all desired fruits.
O best of sages, I shall now relate this to you exactly as the Blessed Lord Śambhu spoke it when questioned by the Daughter of the Mountain.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World as he sat in solitude on Kailāsa, the daughter of Himavat questioned him with devotion.
O Blessed One, O Lord of Gods, what must men do to effortlessly achieve the warding off of all suffering and the accomplishment of every auspiciousness?
Thus addressed by Pārvatī, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose banner bears the bull, related everything that the Blessed One had said to the Goddess; that I shall now relate to you all.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to that great gift called Jambūdvīpa,
just as the Lord Janārdana, whose source is the lotus, has spoken it today.
In the eastern direction, under an auspicious lunar mansion, at a meritorious time in every respect,
during the equinoxes, the solstices, and so forth, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Chapter 5: The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa) [page 336]
Cemādri states:
"One should perform [the rite] during a Vyatīpāta yoga, or especially on one's birthday;
or one should practice the giving of gifts regularly on the eighth or fifteenth lunar day."
A gift should be given in all meritorious places, such as by rivers or temples, or at home, or wherever one was born.

Having diligently honored a Brahmin who is a knower of the Vedas as his preceptor, he should have the Brahmin perform all the necessary rites, such as the smearing of the ground with cow-dung and so forth.
One should smear the entire ground with cow dung mixed with water;
there, one should smear a circular area measuring twenty cubits.
There, O Pārvatī, one should imagine the salt ocean surrounding it on all sides,
measuring one span in width and eight *rognas* in height.
There, one should scatter unbroken grains along with white flowers on all sides;
in the center of that, one should indeed construct Mount Meru out of three bhāras of grain.
In the center, Mount Meru should consist of great rice and be joined with golden *kalpa* trees; to the east, it should be joined with pearls and diamonds.
To the south, with gomedaka and puṣparāga gems.
And afterwards, with emeralds from the Gāruḍa mountain, with sapphires, with Vaiḍūryas, with rubies,
with pieces of white sandalwood, and with corals on all sides—
It should be covered with creepers and have a surface as white as a pearl shell.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight (parvan), there should be white garments;
on the full moon, yellow ones on the right side;
thereafter, on the subsequent days, variegated clothes.
306 Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa,
Chapter 5] And red [threads] on the north, with a thick row [of lamps].
In the center, however, Brahmā should be placed, seated upon a lotus throne,
four-faced, with a body fashioned of gold,
and possessing four arms.
And there he held both a sacrificial ladle and a water-pot.
Likewise, holding a rosary, the implements for recitation, and a black antelope skin upon him,
he caused the Gaṅgā to fall in four streams.
And the fourfold oblation consisting of water and leaves.
Then, having installed the eight world-protectors beginning with Mahendra in their proper order,
one should also [place] various silver images of multitudes of twice-born [brahmins].
And deer should be settled everywhere.
To the east of Mount Mandara, its interior completely surrounded by two white garments as vast as grains of rice,
there is a bull made of gold.
One should perform [the rite] with a dropya tree, provided it is inhabited by deer and birds.
To the south of Mount Gandhamādana,
there is a mountain that should be fashioned with golden jambu trees and shining with the lord of the yakṣas, who is made of gold.
And he was completely enveloped on all sides by yellow garments.
Afterwards, one should place a sesame mountain on top, which has a variegated appearance, is covered with a garment, possesses *pippala* fruits, and is joined with golden swans.
Chapter 5 of the Dānakhaṇḍa:
Cēmādri.
One should cause to be fashioned a large, deep, and fragrant flower.
It was resplendent with a silver spear set with jewels.
Having established that vast mountain to the north,
as well as the Supārśva mountain made of mung beans and fine cloth,
and also the Nyagrodha tree made of gold and the excellent cow.
And having made it auspicious with silver and with [ornaments] fashioned from spears.
One should fashion a flower-ornament for Meru and [represent] the flowing springs of ghee and water in the cardinal directions;
the lakes are made of curds, clarified butter, food, and honey.
And of those [deities], starting from the east, they are arranged in their respective order.
Hima, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Krama, Nīla, and Śveta, endowed with peaks,
extend respectively toward the south and the north for a distance of one prādeśa.
All of them are oriented toward the east and are provided with garments.
In this regard, the wise maintain that the quantity of grain [required] for each of these mountain ranges covered by rain-clouds is measured by their weight;
and all of them are endowed with the power of the wings fashioned by Romaka.
Fragrant flowers, fruits, and pairs of garments should be provided.
Ānīla and Niṣadha extend across [the north], while Mālyavat and Gandhamādana [extend across the south];
Meru is situated in their midst, and those two [latter mountains] are composed of grain.
Niṣadha and Pārijāta are these two boundary mountains;
like Gandhamādana and [Mālyavān], they are each one-fifth the size of Meru.
● There is a variant reading: *prāmāṇyābhātyuparatiḥ*.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5] That mountain Gandhamādana is situated on the eastern side according to the prescribed rule.
Made of white rice, they are situated to the south and north.
All those headed by Sitānta are in the south,
while those headed by Kakubha and Śaṅkhakūṭa are proclaimed to be in the north.
Having made those three Kesara mountains auspiciously out of grain,
O Lord of Mountains, one should wrap Mount Meru and the others with cloths.
The southern region is Bhāratavarṣa, which is surrounded by Kiṃpuruṣa;
beyond that, to the south of Meru, is declared to be Harivarṣa.
Ilāvṛta surrounds Meru; likewise, there are the fourth, Vṛṣabha, as well as Ramya, Hiraṇmaya, and the Northern Kurus.
Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla are situated in the east and west respectively;
thus have the nine regions (varṣas) in Jambudvīpa been described by name.
One should install the Lord of Gods and Śrī within the Himālaya mountains;
these two, fashioned out of gold, should face the temple.
Holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, clad in yellow garments, the infallible one,
wearing a crown and armlets, with his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa.
One should place the goddess to his right, seated in the lotus posture, holding a lotus in her hand, possessing beautiful eyes, and having a serene countenance.
Who could place both me and you in the middle of the assembly?—
me, named Śaṅkara, and you, O fair-faced Gaurī?

One should visualize me as four-armed, seated upon a bull, with matted hair and the moon as a crest-jewel, holding a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
And you, O Mother, who have entered my body, accompanied by the goddess Dīva;
[from the *Dānakhaṇḍa*, Chapter 5: Hemādri].
Upon a splendid throne, [he beheld] the Blessed One, Hari, with the face of a horse.
One should install the golden deity in the form of Kūrma in Bhārata;
Vārāha in Ketumāla, and Matsya in Uttarakuru.
One should place golden or silver [mountains] in their proper order;
thus, having fashioned the continent called Jambūdvīpa according to the prescribed rite.
The half-foot-wash, the seat, and the bath, followed by the ritual installation in due order;
likewise Brahmā and the other gods, the mountains, and the wish-fulfilling trees.
They are worthy of worship with their own name-mantras, illuminated by concluding salutations,
as well as with perfumes, flowers, prostrations, incense, lamps, and fruits.
Likewise, having worshipped with great effort using offerings and other articles,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with clarified butter in the region of Bhadrāśva.
One should offer oblations with the mantras of their respective names, joined with the utterance of "svāhā";
having offered one hundred and ten [oblations] to Brahmā and likewise to Meru.
And for all the others, one should place a hundred and eight oblations (āhutis) and a water-pot (kalaśa) in front of the patron for the purpose of bathing.
One should place fragrant substances and flowers upon its own beard, which is wrapped in cloth and filled with an *āḍhaka* measure, and then insert the tips of *kuśa* grass into it.
Then, one should invoke all those who will bestow spiritual welfare,
as well as all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, the oceans, and the lakes.
"May they come, bringing about the destruction of the sacrificer's misfortunes"—
having thus invoked them, he [should take] the pitcher of pure water belonging to him.
"Thus, 'this has been obtained'— this is the reading in another manuscript.
Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa,
Chapter 5] Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should install it with a spirit of affection.
There, one should bathe the donor, facing eastward, with the waters from the jars.
When the time for giving has arrived, whether it be a woman or a man who is the donor, [they should do so] with the Ṛg-verses dedicated to the goddesses and likewise with the Pāvamānī hymns.
Having been bathed by that preceptor, he should perform an act of giving together with him;
having circumambulated three times, he should take handfuls of flowers in his joined palms.
Having prostrated before each and every mountain in succession,
one should give the central one to the preceptor and recite this mantra;
or else, having obtained his permission, it may be given to someone else.
And just as all the worlds, beginning with the earth, O King of Mountains, are eternally situated in you,
so too are these gods, asuras, and lords of the world.
And the hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, [worship him] eternally.
Through your gift, may I also be liberated from all sins without exception.
O Lord, together with the best of gods, grant me that which is more auspicious than even the king of mountains.
Having spoken thus, one should give to each of the eminent brahmins Mount Meru together with gold, along with a pair of garments made of silver.
One should offer the others in sequence, beginning with the east.
O Mandara mountain, it is true that you were employed by you for the purpose of obtaining the nectar for the gods and the asuras.
The Fifth Chapter on Giving | Hemādri:
And so, protect me from all sides through your grace, so that I may become free from passion (viraja) as you are.
O Lord of Mountains, celebrated as Gandhamādana;
in the Veda, obeisance be to you as Garuḍa. May all my faults and sins be destroyed by being offered to you.
O best of mountains, always provide me with shade.
Salutations to the one who is the fullness of the divine abode, to the immovable one,
to the swan, and to the Person of the Vedas; salutations to the infallible one,
by whom the entire heap of sins has been destroyed through your gift.
Together with Haṃsa, O Amarācala, protect me!
I pay homage to Supārśva, the immovable mountain; I bow eternally to the immeasurable Dhenu and the divine Surabhi.
O you who are endowed with the merit of giving and devotion, through this virtuous act today, I am prostrate before you.
I go to you alone for refuge; know me as such.

Gaurī, fair-complexioned— this is a qualification of Brahmāṇī.

the reading is "aura".)

The recitation by Brahmins, the consecration (*adhivāsanā*), and so forth are included.

In the Matsya Purāṇa: Then, having bathed and wearing white garments, the householder, holding a handful of flowers, [should proceed] amidst auspicious sounds at the conclusion of the fire-oblation and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
One should recite this mantra three times while circumambulating clockwise:
"Homage to the one consisting of the universe; homage to the self of the universal wheel."
You, whose nature is supreme bliss, protect me from the mire of saṃsāra;
for yogis always behold you as this very embodiment of light.
I bow to the reality in the heart that transcends the qualities (guṇas), the wheel of the universe;
the discus resides in Vāsudeva, and Mādhava resides in the center of the discus.
I bow to these two who abide here in a state of mutual support,
because this Viśvamaṇḍala is supreme and removes all sins.
O Āyuva, rescue me from this state of existence;
having been thus addressed, may he, free from envy, bestow the Viśvacakra.

"He shall be served by throngs of apsarases and may remain [there] for three hundred kalpas.

The full presentation of the gift to the preceptor and others, giving to others as well with their permission, the satiation of the poor and the helpless, the performance of the *ekāgni* rite even if the materials are very small, and the arrangement for the distribution among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the preceptor— all this should be performed according to the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*); thereafter, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*).

His lifespan increases constantly and his fortune shall become vast—

Having transcended existence and having become manifest in the world, he does not exist again.

and various fruits— including men, women, cows, elephants, horses, and so forth— are appropriate precisely because they serve as the objects of comparison for the flowers and fruits that constitute their own forms.
"Portions, garments; Suparṇa, birds. Having thus fashioned the ten Kalpalatās upon the altar above the drawn mandala,"
One should place a horse in the center and eight [other figures] in the directions starting from the east.

Salutations again and again to those who destroy sin, who protect the Lord of the World within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

He who performs that which brings about the destruction of the fear of worldly existence.

To her who bestows desired fruits, the giver of wished-for results;
he shall deliver a hundred ancestors from the ocean of existence, his body purified by the destruction of the flood of his misdeeds.
Surrounded by thousands of the wives of the lords of the gods, he is to be saluted by the assembly of lotuses.
Thus,
whoever here recites, remembers, or beholds this ritual for the offering of golden wish-fulfilling vines to the celestial damsels of the quarters, [attains the fruit].
O Purandara, do not abandon me; let this life of mine not perish.

Now, the fourteenth great gift (mahādāna), known as the Seven Oceans, is described.
The Fish [Incarnation] said:

Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift known as Saptasāgaraka, which destroys even the most heinous sins. Having reached an auspicious day and performed the recitation by Brahmins, one should proceed.

as well as the preparation of the sacrificial priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, the ornaments, the coverings, and so forth.

measuring either one span (*prādeśa*) or one cubit (*aratni*).

One should prepare seven palas of liquorice, or as much as possible up to a thousand palas;
and all these should be placed upon a black antelope skin over sesame seeds.

The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and vessels (bhāṇḍas) are to be measured by the span (prādeśa) and other units, which are to be understood as horizontal measures of wool. A span (prādeśa) is equal to twenty-one finger-joints; half of that is a thumb-breadth (aṅguṣṭha). Sesame seeds and gold coins are to be used as the basis for the measurement of the black antelope skins (kṛṣṇājina).
They should be measured by a *droṇa*, as their extent is seen to be such;
first, the wise man should fill the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with salt.
The second [offering] is with milk, and the third again is with clarified butter.
The fourth [offering] is with jaggery alone, the fifth with curd,
the sixth with sugar, and the seventh with water from a sacred pilgrimage site.
One should place a beautiful golden image of Brahmā at the edge of the salt,

One should place Bhāskara in the midst of molasses, Surādhipa in the midst of curd, Lakṣmī upon sugar, and Pārvatī in the midst of water;
all the jewels and grains everywhere.

The characteristics of the images of Brahmā and the other deities have been stated; all the gems and all the grains [to be used] in the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa have been explained in the technical definitions (paribhāṣā).
One should likewise provide the measurements for the Tulāpuruṣa and other [gifts] here as well.
Then, at the conclusion of the Vāru oblation, he was sown by the preeminent knowers of the Vedas.
Having circumambulated three times clockwise, one should recite these mantras.

By the word "remainder" (śeṣa), one should understand the recitation for a "day of merit" (puṇyāhavācana), the giving of water and the aforementioned gifts to the preceptor and others, as well as the giving of gifts to those who follow him, the satiation of the poor and the helpless, and the performance of the single-fire rite (ekāgnividhāna) when resources are meager. This is the specific detail: on the second day, the Tulā-puru-
The Section on Giving (Dānakhaṇḍa), Chapter 5. Hemādri:

Upon the completion of the remainder of the prescribed rites, before the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation), one should perform a *vāruṇahoma* (oblation to Varuṇa) with clarified butter and sesame seeds, reciting the mantra associated with him one thousand times:
"Salutations to you, the eternal foundations of all rivers."
Salutations again and again to the oceans from which living beings and the breath of life emerge.
Since you gladden the inhabitants of the three worlds with the nectar of your essence— consisting of milk, water, curd, honey, salt, sugar, and ambrosia—
and further satisfy them with riches;
Therefore, please grant me the complete destruction of my sins as well.
For in all the worlds, you alone possess a multitude of jewels firmly bound by the gods, asuras, and sages,
serving as the cleansing water for ablutions, the ointment for the sky, and the ornament.
"May that which is for the world also be for me; may there be prosperity.

Then, at the conclusion of the formal gift accompanied by a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity, one should perform, as before, the invocation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the deities, and their dismissal (*visarjana*).
Thus, filled with long-standing wonder, he gives away oceans here that consist of the essence of gold and are joined with nectar. He bestows these which possess the color of pure, refined gold.
He attains the station of Hari, surrounded by immortals.
Resplendent with the destruction of all sins, he is fully capable of [rescuing] his father, grandfather, son, and wife,
even if they are crowded within the world of hell.
With the sound "ṛk," he reaches the abode of Śiva.

Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5] Now,
the fifteenth great gift (mahādāna), known as the Jewel-Cow (Ratnadhenu), is set forth.

"Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift (mahādāna).

for here [are included] the worship of the place, time, prosperity, and Śiva and others, as well as the recitation by Brahmins.

The meaning is that one should fashion the form of a cow with its calf using lines;
a wise person should place eighty-one rubies in the mouth.

a golden tilaka on the forehead, and a hundred pearls for the eyes.

It is known from the principle that "the specific fruit [of an action] depends on its substance and its measure"— as in the case of the nose, the first part of the month, or gold tilakas and the like— that the performance should be carried out according to one's capacity, with the pearl ornaments divided and placed upon the two eyes.
A hundred pieces of coral are situated upon the pair of eyebrows, two pearl-shells on the two ears,
golden horns, and a head consisting of a hundred diamonds.
"He sings with horns"— this plural is used in reference to the horns of the calves.
[Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 5]
Hemādri states:
On the neck is a jeweled band consisting of one hundred *gomedaka* gems;
on the back are one hundred *indranīla* sapphires, and on the two sides are one hundred *vaidūrya* cat's-eyes.
The belly should be made of crystal, containing within it a hundred *saugandhika* flowers;
the hooves should be made of gold, and the tail should consist of strings of pearls.

Regarding the word "sphaṭikaiḥ" (with crystals), it should be understood from the context of association and the expression "tadvat" (like that) as being "one hundred" in number; likewise, "saugandhika" is a specific kind of ruby, and it should also be understood that the pearls are likewise one hundred in number.

One should imagine a hundred *gārutmata* gems in the *apāna* [channel],
and likewise, one should place other jewels in all the joints.
One should place other gems, such as rubies and the like, according to one's capacity and availability.
One should fashion the tongue from sugar, the cow-dung from jaggery,
the cow-urine from clarified butter, and likewise the curd and milk in their natural forms.
At the tip of the tail, one should place a chowrie; nearby, a copper milking vessel;
and golden earrings as well as ornaments according to one's means.

Having performed the arrangement in this manner, one should then carry out the consecration of the fire-pit (adhivāsana).

Those who give fertile land to a twice-born man learned in the Vedas,

"O Lord of the Gods, O Master, I consider nothing to be superior to the gift of land,

The five ancestors beginning with the father, and the six who are connected to the earth—

O Purandara, he who gives the earth filled with jewels is liberated from all impurities and is glorified in the heavenly world.
The king who bestows the vast earth, endowed with all desirable qualities, becomes a sovereign over kings; such a gift is unsurpassed.

That thousand-eyed man who gives here the earth that milks all desires, preceded by the fulfillment of every wish, goes to heaven.

By the gift of land, a king is liberated from all sin;
indeed, no other gift excels the gift of land.
O Purandara, for him who gives land that is fertile and of sweet soil,
the worlds acquired through the merit of the gift of land never perish.
In every way, O Śakra, a king who desires prosperity and seeks happiness in this world must always bestow land upon a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rites.
Even after committing a sin, a man who gives land to a twice-born man casts off that sin,

Cemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa, Chapter 7] The oceans, rivers, mountains, and various sacred fords— these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a gift of land.
Therefore, O King, having obtained [the land], a wise man should indeed give it to a Brahmin;

Having performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with self-restraint and accompanied by sacrificial fees,
one does not obtain that fruit which one attains from the gift of land.
The donor benefits ten generations;
likewise, one who seizes land previously given goes to hell by depriving those ten.
He who does not give after having promised, or who takes back what has been given—

Those who seize the earth are born as black snakes dwelling in dried-out hollows within the waterless forests of Vindhya;
they shed tears as they weep, miserable and deprived of their refuge.
If the field of Brahmins is seized, they shall destroy the family for three generations.
Those who bestow the earth, taking with them one who maintains the sacred fires, along with servants and beloved guests, do not approach Yama.
Likewise: "A land constantly filled with sugarcane, barley, wheat, and rice;
abounding in cattle and vehicles, and acquired through great effort."
By giving land containing seeds and provided with all kinds of precious treasures, one obtains inexhaustible worlds; for that is his "land-sacrifice" (bhūmisatra).
Having shaken off all impurity, a king shall be honored by the virtuous;
he who bestows the earth is glorified by the good in this world.
Just as that drop of oil, O Śakra, spreads when it has fallen—

Devoted to dance and song, adorned with divine garlands,

And he who properly bestows land here upon a twice-born according to the prescribed rite rejoices happily in heaven, honored by gods and gandharvas.
And a hundred apsarases, adorned with divine garlands,
attend upon the giver of earth in the world of Brahmā, O Lord of Gods.
Beings always attend upon the man who gives land:
the conch shell, the auspicious throne, the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the excellent elephant.
From the gift of land come merits as well as heaps of gold;
furthermore, one's command becomes forever unimpeded and the sound of victory arises.
O Purandara, the flowers of the gift of land are its fruit, which is heaven;
its medicinal herbs have gold for their blossoms, and its grassy meadows are made of gold and kusha grass.
A person who gives land attains the ground from which nectar springs;
there is no gift equal to land, and there is no teacher equal to sacrifice.
There is no dharma superior to truth, and there is no treasure equal to generosity;
having realized this, Vāsava [ruled] over this earth, O descendant of Aṅgiras.
Then he gave to Aṅgiras a cow adorned with excellent jewels.
Whoever causes this praise of the gift of land to be heard in an assembly,
for him there shall be no share among the Rākṣasas, nor indeed among the Asuras.
And there would be no doubt that it would be offered as an accumulation for the ancestors.
Devala says: "The gift of land has been declared by the twice-born to be the most excellent among all gifts."
Having gone there, a person is honored in heaven by the best of the thirty gods.

It delivers even the twice-born who accepts the gift;

Moreover, whatever small amount of joy is bestowed by her with even a mere three-fold stroke of the rod, that indeed shall be experienced right here and now in this very world.
Furthermore, by the gift of land, the fruit of all gifts is obtained;
they are blessed, they are virtuous, and they have achieved their life's purpose—of this there is no doubt.

By that very act, a person certainly attains the fruit of the gift of land.

by giving a field of vegetables, a man shall obtain the world of Aṅgiras.

he who gives a reservoir of water for the sake of water shall attain the world of Dāruṇa.
That horse belongs to whichever deity for whose sake it was intended;
having given the pleasure garden to that deity, he rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
Having given that which originates from a mine of jewels, one is honored in the world of Śakra.

O twice-born ones, that best of men who indeed bestows a collyrium-mine and land is honored by his ancestors in the world of Yama.

The best of men, having given land with its sprouting vegetation to the Lord Śikhīśa, attains the world of the Sādhyas; there is no doubt to be entertained in this matter.

A man who gives a field of sugarcane or even a field of rice attains great merit and goes to the world of Brahmā.

Even if one has transgressed by only a single finger’s breadth due to negligence or delusion, O Supreme Person, that offense regarding the Dharma persists for many thousands of years.

Just as Viṣṇu, the causal Puruṣa, is the most excellent among the gods,

Chapter 8 of the Dānakhaṇḍa:

O King, the householder’s stage of life should always be pursued by men who have attained their desires, for therein virtue, wealth, and pleasure are found together, as is renowned fame.

Those days are truly counted which pass in the householder's stage of life;

Having gratified the two divine Aśvins, she is born endowed with beauty.
Viṣṇu said:
By giving ghee to Brahmins every day throughout the entire month of Āśvina and thereby pleasing the two Aśvins, one becomes possessed of beauty; [this result is attained] in that very month.
By feeding Brahmins daily with cow-products (gorasa), one becomes endowed with health; likewise,
by offering oblations into the fire daily with sesame seeds during the month of Māgha and feeding Brahmins with rice cooked in ghee (ghṛtakulmāṣa), one’s [digestive] fires become kindled.
The wise one said:
"A man who gives sesame seeds indeed obtains his desired offspring;
this is especially true in the month of Māgha, and even more so when mixed with iron."
In the Mahābhārata: "He who gives sesame seeds to Brahmins in the month of Māgha does not behold the hell crowded with all kinds of beings."
Thus concludes the procedure for monthly gifts. Now follow the gifts according to the seasons, as stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:

58-1 The giving of food, ointments, and so forth is desired in the spring;
likewise, the giving of drinks is in the summer, and that of clothing immediately thereafter.

That goddess is indeed quickly pleased by that vidyā.
[As stated] in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"O Dharma, in autumn, even by the wearing of garments..."
Having offered the gift of sacrificial grass (barhis) at the rising of the sun, a man [attains merit].

Yama says:
Having fed brahmins with *kamaras* out of devotion during the winter,

Hemādri: [The Section on Gifts, Chapter 12]. Now, the seasonal gifts (*ṛtudāna*).

Chapter Thirteen:
Now, the gifts that yield infinite fruit.
By which the ponds, delightful with groves and with serpents sporting in the waves of their surrounding shores, surpass the graceful movement of the horses of the sun’s chariot;

Hemādri: [Dānakhaṇḍa,

Dānakhaṇṇḍa, Chapter 12: Hemādri.
Health is the means for attaining virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
therefore, by the gift of health, a man becomes endowed with all these at all times.
He establishes a hospital, well-stocked with great medicinal herbs,

The physician, however, should be learned in the scriptures, possessed of life-force, having witnessed the efficacy of remaining medicines,
knowing the names and colors of medicinal roots, and knowing the proper time for extraction.

He is one who knows the elements, what is wholesome, and the sacrifice; he is tireless in knowing the primary causes, the premonitory signs of diseases, and the subsequent methods of treatment.
Likewise, one who knows the science of medicine according to place, time, and procedure;
one who is a knower of the eight-limbed Āyurveda; and one who knows the application of medicinal formulations for the fist-clenching technique. There are eight limbs of Āyurveda.

81. 1. Just as [the branches of medicine] are stated by Suśruta to be: Śālākya (treatment of the head and neck), Kāyacikitsā (internal medicine), Bhūtavidyā (demonology), Kaumārabhṛtya (pediatrics), Agadatantra (toxicology), Rasāyaṇatantra (rejuvenation therapy), and Vājīkaraṇatantra (aphrodisiacs).

He who, by means of very slight expedients, can liberate those afflicted by disease— those whose conditions vary through the accumulation and diminution of wind, bile, phlegm, and the rest.

Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who is endowed with all necessary requisites.
Since health is the means for achieving virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, therefore,

Then, by diligently establishing even a single learned person in a state of well-being,

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, all the gods, diseases, kinsmen, and kings—these are the great obstacles to yoga; they are not [obstacles] for yogis.

Having protected the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who were afflicted by disease.

Just as no end of space can be found even by the gods,

By this great merit, having gone to the city of Śiva,

Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage and accompanied by his servants,

Then, having always attained [this state] through the remainder of his own dharma and remaining ever self-restrained,

"Dispassionate toward knowledge and having resorted to meditation on the Self, one who abandons his own body like a blade of grass shall reach the end of all suffering;

One who is completely fulfilled in every respect is designated as "liberated."
Therefore, for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should treat those afflicted by disease,
especially the lords of yogis, with both body and wealth.
A wise man should never despise those who are sick, nor even those who are weak;
for it is from them that sin constantly arises, like a blind man stumbling.
Thinking himself to be possessed by a deity day after day, he approaches [the sick] like one afflicted by disease; thus does the ocean of worldly existence become a source of suffering.

Now follow the gifts that remove disease.

O best of sages, being thus addressed by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, I shall tell you everything that the Blessed One said to him.
Mental anxieties and physical ailments indeed cause the emaciation of the body;
one who desires their own welfare should perform meritorious deeds for the sake of avoiding them.
Fever and diarrhea, consumption, abdominal tumors, colic, fistula-in-ano, leprosy,
diseases of the digestive fire, wind-disorders, throat-spasm, and smallpox;
In diseases of the throat, teeth, and tongue, as well as in diseases of the head and the upajihvikā (ranula),

Knots, dysuria, bladder diseases, and abdominal enlargement—
these and many others, possessing great speed and great strength.
Diseases, numbering one hundred, are indeed the causes of death;
whatever may bring about the pacification of a particular disease, that should be performed by the wise.
Medicine, recitation, burnt offerings, and the like; charity, worship of the deities, and so forth—all these are said to be the "excellent gift" (sauvarṇa-dāna) that pacifies every disease.
That [iron] is prescribed for smallpox and for pulmonary consumption;

By applying these as an ointment, they pacify all ailments arising in the rectum in every respect.

by giving cloth dyed with safflower, one attains great fortune.
By the gift of cloth dyed with saffron, one attains great beauty.
